  • According to recent reports, the report — the 2026 edition of "Challenges to Security in Space" — is the third iteration of the DIA's unclassified intelligence assessment on space-related challenges and threats to U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last month, the U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) released a chilling and info-packed report judging the scope and breadth of threats posed by the nation's adversaries in space.

The latest report focuses on China, Russia and the emerging space powers of Iran and North Korea. It looks at what's happening in Earth orbit and beyond, including cislunar space, the region between our planet and the moon.

According to recent reports, the report — the 2026 edition of "Challenges to Security in Space" — is the third iteration of the DIA's unclassified intelligence assessment on space-related challenges and threats to U.S. national security, as well as the extent to which space is treated internationally as a warfighting domain.

Information within the report, which you can read here, is current as of July 2026. DIA's mission is to provide intelligence on foreign militaries to help prevent wars, and win the ones that are fought.

The report's up-front finding is that China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea are developing, testing, deploying and using space capabilities "in a way that threatens the security of all space systems and their associated space benefits.".

Indeed, China and Russia are developing "a formidable spectrum" of offensive capabilities to degrade or destroy space services of other countries, from kinetic destruction to sophisticated jamming and cyber operations.

The DIA report also notes that "the production of cheaper, smaller, and simpler satellites, which are faster to develop and deploy, along with the expansion of commercially available launch services, are driving the rapid integration of commercial space alternatives to support national security.".

While space commercialization is making previously government-centered space services widely available to interested parties, the DIA report adds, that availability also includes state and non-state actors with malign interests.

A major item dealt with by the DIA is "counterspace" — and it's not the kind that you'll find in your kitchen.

According to recent reports, counterspace operations can be either offensive or defensive. They can be used on purpose to reversibly or irreversibly deny, disrupt, degrade, damage or destroy a space object or component of a space system.

Here are the key elements of counterspace, as identified within the DIA report:.

The DIA report underscores that Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon.

Russia is doing so despite its obligation to comply with the 1967 Outer Space Treaty. That U.N. agreement prohibits the placement of any objects carrying nuclear weapons, or any other kinds of weapons of mass destruction, into orbit around Earth.

"A space-based capability such as this could cause rapid and sudden loss or degradation of thousands of satellites operated by countries and companies around the world," the DIA report states, "as well as to the vital communications, navigation, scientific, meteorological, commercial and national security services they provide.".

A nuclear detonation in space could be tailored to impact satellites in most orbits, the DIA report warns, from low Earth orbit for commercial and reconnaissance satellites, geosynchronous orbit for critical communications, and medium Earth orbit for navigation and timing satellites.

Recent findings suggest that the newly issued DIA report also observes that exploring cislunar space is of increasing interest to spacefaring nations for potential scientific and economic opportunities. However, nations such as China "may be exploring military applications from cislunar space," the report notes.

China has stated its goal of developing a cislunar space economy by 2045.

Industry observers note that "China is also the first country to attempt sustained operations on the far side of the moon, with numerous projects slated to support that effort through the next decade. China portrays its interest in cislunar space as peaceful, but PRC [People's Republic of China] officials have also discussed pursuing military capabilities in cislunar space," the report states.

Placing a keen eye on the DIA report is Peter Garretson, a senior fellow in defense studies at the American Foreign Policy Council and a strategy consultant who focuses on space and defense.

In a recent development, according to Garretson, the most significant positive change from earlier DIA appraisals is the explicit assessment that Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon. He told Space.com that the DIA's expanded treatment of the threat of a nuclear weapon on orbit reflects concerns in the Congress and the Trump White House.

However, Garretson also flagged what he noted is a consequential omission in the report: the disappearance of the prior treatment (in the 2022 version of the report) of research competition, surveillance beyond geosynchronous Earth orbit and the potential military use of deep space for staging reserve forces.

In Garretson's view, the DIA needs to help put the puzzle pieces together for Congress and the attentive public about what exactly China is doing, and how it fits together in the nation's strategy to achieve comprehensive space dominance.

According to Garretson, "everything they are doing, from launch cadence, reusable launch, commercial space investment, investments in power, propulsion, repair, manufacturing, to commercial assets working together" supports both an economic expansion toward fresh resources and what China hopes will be overwhelming military power and strategic depth.

Sources indicate that garretson senses the moves by China to develop extractive and in-space industries "is truly the strategic threat that could crush American space power. Now is the time to be making the investments to ensure we have a 'freedom's forge' and 'arsenal of democracy' in space that can protect the open space commerce that is the nation's strategy.".

As for the DIA's outlook for the future: The agency concluded that space almost certainly will remain an increasingly competitive and crowded environment as space capabilities improve and other countries seize opportunities in the final frontier.

"The increase of Chinese, Russian, Iranian and North Korean counterspace capabilities, rapid growth in the number of space objects, and the proliferation of requirements for space-enabled services," the DIA report states, "will all complicate operations in space in the coming decade.".

Vitamin C could help block cancer-linked chemicals in your stomach, study finds

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (729 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vitamin C may do more than support everyday health.
  • Exposure to nitrates and nitrites has increased in North American diets over the past several decades.
  • Sources indicate that one of these reactions, called nitrosation, can produce substances that researchers suspect may contribute to cancer development.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vitamin C may do more than support everyday health. Latest research from the University of Waterloo suggests that it could also help prevent potentially cancer-causing chemicals from forming during digestion. Using mathematical modeling, scientists investigated how vitamin C influences chemical reactions in the digestive system that have been linked to cancer risk.

Exposure to nitrates and nitrites has increased in North American diets over the past several decades. These compounds are found in cured meats such as bacon and salami, as well as in fruits and vegetables grown in soil or water affected by pollution. Although nitrates and nitrites contribute to key functions in the brain and cardiovascular system, they can also participate in potentially harmful reactions once they reach the stomach.

Sources indicate that one of these reactions, called nitrosation, can produce substances that researchers suspect may contribute to cancer development. Understanding what causes these chemicals to form, and what might prevent their formation, has been a longstanding challenge.

Why Vitamin C Could Change the Cancer Risk Equation.

Recent findings suggest that "Since at least the 90s, researchers have been studying the link between cancer and these compounds, with conflicting results," said Dr. Gordon McNicol, a post-doctoral researcher in applied mathematics and the first author of the study. "Our work suggests that the presence of dietary Vitamin C may help explain these inconsistencies.".

In a recent development, to investigate this possibility, the researchers developed a mathematical model that simulates how nitrates and nitrites travel through the body and undergo chemical changes. The model incorporated several interconnected systems, including the salivary glands, stomach, small intestine, and plasma, the liquid portion of blood.

It has been revealed that their simulations revealed that vitamin C consumed alongside nitrates and nitrites may interfere with the formation of potentially harmful compounds. This could help explain why foods containing nitrates do not necessarily carry the same risks.

It has been revealed that for example, leafy vegetables such as spinach naturally contain both nitrates and vitamin C. According to the model, the presence of vitamin C could limit the chemical reactions associated with cancer risk, potentially helping explain the protective effects suggested by some dietary research.

Could Taking Vitamin C After Meals Help?

The researchers also explored whether vitamin C supplements might offer similar benefits when taken after eating.

Their findings suggest that taking vitamin C after each meal could moderately reduce the formation of nitrosation products associated with cancer risk. This effect could be particularly relevant when consuming foods containing nitrates and nitrites, including processed meats such as bacon and salami.

In a recent development, however, the results come from mathematical simulations rather than clinical trials. Although the model predicts that vitamin C can reduce the production of potentially harmful chemicals, further research is needed to determine whether this translates into a measurable reduction in cancer risk in humans.

Upcoming Clues for Future Cancer Prevention Research.

The researchers believe their model could help scientists better understand the complicated relationship between diet, digestive chemistry, and cancer risk. It may also provide guidance for future experiments examining how nutritional choices influence the formation of potentially harmful compounds.

"This work provides a mechanistic roadmap for future clinical and laboratory studies by identifying the key interacting drivers of these potentially harmful chemical reactions, including nitrite exposure, antioxidant intake, meal timing, gastric conditions and oral microbiome activity," stated Dr. Anita Layton, professor of applied mathematics and Canada 150 researcher chair. "This model can help researchers design more targeted experiments and interventions, focusing on when and in whom nitrosation is most likely to occur.".

By identifying how factors such as vitamin C intake, meal timing, stomach conditions, and bacteria in the mouth interact, the model could help researchers develop more precise strategies for studying and potentially reducing cancer-related chemical reactions during digestion.

The study, "Vitamin C as a nitrosation inhibitor: A modelling study across dietary patterns and water quality," was published in the Journal of Theoretical Biology.

#47726. Industry News: Regular Tech Bros Are Worried About Honeypots

Industry News: Regular Tech Bros Are Worried About Honeypots

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1166 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when the founder of a cybersecurity firm hired Blaine Anderson as a matchmaker, it wasn’t just because the man was lonely.
  • In a recent development, the cybersecurity founder isn’t the only one.
  • “Even if you're not a CEO or at a substantial tech giant, these fears have trickled down to just regular professionals,” Simone Grossman, a Brooklyn-based matchmaker, tells WIRED.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when the founder of a cybersecurity firm hired Blaine Anderson as a matchmaker, it wasn’t just because the man was lonely. It was also, Anderson states, because he was “super worried about spies.”.

In a recent development, the cybersecurity founder isn’t the only one. As Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security dominates headlines and AI companies reportedly warn employees against “honeypots,” matchmakers say that more men with pretty normal lives are worried that their dates may have ulterior motives: accessing corporate secrets.

“Even if you're not a CEO or at a substantial tech giant, these fears have trickled down to just regular professionals,” Simone Grossman, a Brooklyn-based matchmaker, tells WIRED.

One tech worker, who requested anonymity in order to speak candidly, says he considers himself “highly selective” about the people he interacts with face-to-face.

“Even though I could vet you from looking you up online, I can't help but still be a tad dubious,” he tells WIRED. On a scale from zero to 10, with 10 being the most anxious about espionage, he puts himself at a seven.

In a recent development, even though the vast majority of tech employees likely won’t be targeted for romantic espionage, matchmakers say more clients have lately expressed concerns about women exploiting them for their corporate secrets. One Palantir employee told Andersen he wouldn’t date anyone who was a Chinese or Russian national. The anxiety has even become a marketing opportunity: One firm is pitching its latest line of AI executive girlfriends as a “zero espionage” alternative to human dating.

The concern isn’t entirely without basis. Some companies hire consultants to advise executives and lower-level employees with access to sensitive information on security risks, including the possibility of honeypots. Several of these consultants tell WIRED that raising the subject can be awkward.

“This one is always a very difficult message to deliver—to explain to, say, very sensitive engineers that maybe they're getting a lot of email attention because of their job,” says Isaac Stone Fish, founder and chief executive of the business intelligence firm Strategy Risks, “as opposed to the charm and force of their personality.”.

In a recent development, amy Andersen, founder of Silicon Valley matchmaking company Linx Dating (and no relation to Blaine Anderson), notes that for clients concerned about their romantic partners’ intentions, she offers background checks, personal vetting, and NDAs. The security features are part of her “bespoke” packages that range anywhere from $75,000 to more than $500,000 for the “Founders Level.”.

Sources indicate that fear of romantic espionage is just the latest manifestation of growing distrust in the dating world. Shannon Lundgren, a matchmaker who has worked in San Francisco for 15 years, says that while she hasn’t necessarily heard more concerns about honeypots, she has noticed heightened skepticism around dating in general, as well as growing concerns about privacy.

The anxiety is particularly acute among AI workers, whose net worths—and therefore their perceived romantic desirability—are on the rise.

“If you're somebody who is a little bit shy or who is maybe a very stereotypical engineer type, to suddenly have your market value in the dating world change so drastically—you're already suspicious,” Grossman claims.

To be worried about corporate espionage on top of all that, she indicates, is “a mind fuck.”.

Honeypots and their state or corporate sponsors often look for “signs of vulnerability, such as an unhappy marriage, or someone seeking “excitement or adventure,” says Ira Winkler, a security consultant and the chief information security officer in residence at identity protection tech giant Cloaked. Lonely people are opportune targets, regardless of marriage or relationship status.

The advice security experts give is somewhat obvious: If it seems too good to be true, it probably is.

“Really, if a beautiful woman approaches you, you know it's not for your personality,” Winkler tells his clients.

When tech workers do think of honeypots, they may gravitate toward the stereotype of a beautiful stranger who seduces someone at a bar and then extracts company secrets. “Any time one of us would take a trip to Asia, someone would always make a comment about getting a foreign girlfriend, or future wife, etc.,” one tech worker tells WIRED about his experience at a majority-male workplace. “We'd joke about them meeting a spy, but nobody really considered that seriously. Mostly they were just thinking of sex.”.

That setup is largely a misconception. In reality, according to Greg Rinckey, founding partner of the legal services and consulting firm Tully Rinckey, most honeypot victims are groomed over time. “We’re talking sometimes months, could be years, where they're fostering that relationship,” he says. Rinckey compares it to scammers trying to keep victims on the phone: The longer someone talks to another person and feels they know them, the more likely they are to trust them with sensitive information.

In a recent development, catherine Marinis-Yaqub, a principal at the crisis and security consulting group Control Risks, tells WIRED that when people imagine the beautiful stranger at a bar, they may miss more likely scenarios, like an unexpected guest at a business meeting, a savvy networker at an industry conference, or a flirt at someone’s favorite coffee shop. Jensen Huang met Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese asset, for example, through a mutual business associate (who, according to The Wall Street Journal, also happened to be Alice’s husband).

For the man too scared of spies to make contact with a human romantic partner, there’s always artificial intelligence.

On Tuesday, in the wake of the Huang scandal, AI-relationship platform Joi AI introduced a suite of "zero espionage" Executive Girlfriends. Brand director Julie Levin describes Joi AI as a “safe space” for exploration, where owners can exchange NSFW texts, images, and videos with AI companions without judgment or rejection.

It made sense, she says, to extend that sense of security to honeypot-phobia.

“If they have some business secrets they don't want to share on a date or they feel nervous discussing with real people,” Levin claims, “they can discuss them comfortably with their AIs.” (Levin assures WIRED that Joi AI employs several layers of security and that all of the data is anonymized.).

High-profile executives are among those most at risk of honeypots, notes Winkler, the security consultant. They can also be some of the hardest to protect.

“It's really hard to influence somebody who's in control of the organization and just happens to be a sleazebag,” Winkler notes.

Industry observers note that it’s particularly difficult, notes Rinckey, when bosses think they’re the smartest person in the room and consider themselves immune to manipulation. It’s also not easy, he says, to be in the position of challenging an executive.

Industry observers note that “Cocky, arrogant, and boisterous” chief executives make for desirable targets because “they love to talk about their business, and they love to talk about themselves,” Rinckey indicates. In these situations, he says, “you don't even really have to pry them that much.”.

Disney beats fourth-quarter estimates, targets $3 billion in savings through cost-cutting efforts

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Disney on Tuesday reported quarterly earnings and revenue that exceeded analysts' expectations and declared it's targeting $3 billion in cost savings by fiscal 2029.
  • Sources indicate that those cost-cutting efforts include several rounds of layoffs declared in recent months, Disney's chief financial officer, Hugh Johnston, told CNBC.
  • Future cost-saving measures will include reductions in administrative and other general expenses, Johnston stated, while adding, "We do expect more layoffs.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disney on Tuesday reported quarterly earnings and revenue that exceeded analysts' expectations and declared it's targeting $3 billion in cost savings by fiscal 2029.

Sources indicate that those cost-cutting efforts include several rounds of layoffs declared in recent months, Disney's chief financial officer, Hugh Johnston, told CNBC. The most recent round, which seeks to reduce costs by up to 20%, was reported earlier this month.

Future cost-saving measures will include reductions in administrative and other general expenses, Johnston stated, while adding, "We do expect more layoffs.".

Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro told investors on the tech giant's earnings call that the job cuts are "not easy.".

"They affect people who care deeply about Disney and have contributed so much to this manufacturer," he noted. "At the same time, these steps are vital if we want to be a company that moves faster, adapts to a rapidly changing environment, and keeps investing in the content and technology that will drive our growth.".

The cuts will help Disney fund its $26 billion in projected content spend for fiscal 2027, a 9% increase from fiscal 2026.

The entertainment giant is also forecasting double-digit growth in earnings per share in the next fiscal year, as well as segment operating income growth of around 8%.

Disney noted that the majority of that growth will be concentrated in the first half of the year due to the theatrical debut of "Avengers: Doomsday" and a boost from the Super Bowl, which will air on Disney's ESPN and ABC networks.

"The growth is really going to come in the first half of this year," Johnston said. "That's the opposite of what we saw in '26, where the growth was backloaded.".

Recent findings suggest that the tech giant will also increase its annual dividend to $2 a share, a 33% increase from the previously declared dividend. It will be payable in two installments of $1 per share, one in January and one in July.

It has been revealed that here's how Disney performed in its fiscal fourth quarter ended Oct. 3, compared with what Wall Street expected, according to LSEG:.

Disney reported net income for the fiscal fourth quarter of $2.61 billion, or $1.51 per share, compared with $1.31 billion, or 73 cents per share, during the same period the year prior.

Adjusting for one-time items, including severance and other restructuring charges as well as the value of intangible assets, Disney reported earnings per share of $1.77.

The company's revenue for the quarter was 16% higher year over year, and results were once again lifted by its parks and streaming divisions.

Industry observers note that disney's experiences segment, which includes its theme parks and cruises, reported nearly $10.11 billion in revenue, up 15% year over year. Operating income for the unit increased 20% to $2.25 billion.

The division is already a top performer for the manufacturer, but it benefited in the fiscal fourth quarter because of an extra calendar week compared with the previous fiscal year.

While international attendance continues to lag at Disney's domestic parks, it is being offset by domestic attendance, especially at the Walt Disney World resort in Orlando, Florida, Johnston remarked.

Growth at Disneyland Paris was driven by recent investments including an expansion area called World of Frozen. Attendance at the Hong Kong and Shanghai parks remained soft because of broad economic challenges in those regions, according to Disney.

Still, D'Amaro said he believes the growth in parks will be sustainable through next year, especially with new additions, including the "Monsters, Inc."-themed land "Monstropolis" opening at Walt Disney World in 2027.

"Q1 forward resort bookings at Walt Disney World are pacing up compared to the prior year," he stated. "And new capacity and new experiences will start coming online in 2027. We keep investing to make the experience fresh, and what we see is that drives repeat visits.".

Sources indicate that the organization expects operating income for the experiences segment to grow in the high-single digits in fiscal 2027. Growth is expected to be front-loaded as the company laps the launch of the Disney Adventure cruise ship, which set sail in March.

Over at its entertainment division, Disney saw revenue increase 17% to $11.89 billion. Operating income nearly doubled to $1.33 billion.

Revenue from streaming, specifically, rose 19% to $6.1 billion, Disney remarked.

It has been revealed that the segment benefited from the extra week on the fiscal calendar as well as from growth in subscription and affiliate fees. Additionally, the company saw higher theatrical distribution revenue from titles like "Toy Story 5.".

Disney said Tuesday it expects operating income for the entertainment division to grow in the high-single digits in the coming fiscal year.

According to recent reports, the tech giant's sports division saw revenue increase 16% in the fiscal fourth quarter, reaching $4.61 billion. Operating income for the segment surged more than 50% to $1.39 billion.

Subscription and affiliate fees fueled this growth alongside an increase in advertising revenue.

Sources indicate that the tech giant expects its sports division's operating income to grow by double digits in fiscal 2027. It noted that the fiscal first quarter of the year will see some declines because of the timing of College Football Playoff games and the Upcoming Year's window. However, the fiscal second quarter will benefit from the college championship as well as the broadcast of Super Bowl 61.

Disney's outlook for overall and segment results for fiscal 2027 excludes the impact of a 53rd week in fiscal 2026.

In a recent development, D'Amaro has made advancing technology a pillar of the organization's growth strategy. In September, Disney hired Karandeep Anand in the newly created position of chief technology officer.

"Technology is central to how we connect fans to more of Disney and drive returns on our investment," D'Amaro mentioned on the earnings call. "[Anand has] been energized by how much opportunity he sees to move faster and go further in product and technology. Done right, that means serving our fans even better, working more efficiently and being more innovative across every one of our businesses.".

Disney revealed a partnership with Adobe earlier this month to develop generative artificial intelligence models.

D'Amaro told investors that the team is exploring ways to use AI to make booking trips to Disney parks easier.

A hidden biological divide may help explain Alzheimer’s and chronic pain

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Emerging research suggests that biological sex and genetics may play a major role in how neurological disorders develop, progress, and respond to treatment.
  • Researchers are increasingly finding that certain neurological conditions can behave differently depending on a person's biological sex and genetic makeup.
  • Two of the latest studies highlight how menopause and inherited genetic factors may influence Alzheimer's vulnerability and treatment responses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Emerging research suggests that biological sex and genetics may play a major role in how neurological disorders develop, progress, and respond to treatment. The findings, which will be presented at Neuroscience 2026, reveal notable differences that could help researchers develop more personalized approaches to treating complex brain conditions. Neuroscience 2026 is the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and the world's largest source of emerging news about brain science and health.

Researchers are increasingly finding that certain neurological conditions can behave differently depending on a person's biological sex and genetic makeup. Understanding these differences could lead to treatments better suited to each individual's biology. Two conditions receiving particular attention are Alzheimer's disease (AD), an incurable disorder that progressively damages memory and other brain functions, and fibromyalgia, a chronic illness marked by persistent pain and fatigue that affects 2-4% of the global population. According to the World Health Organization, Alzheimer's affects between 35 and 40 million people worldwide.

Menopause, Genetics, and Alzheimer's Disease.

Two of the latest studies highlight how menopause and inherited genetic factors may influence Alzheimer's vulnerability and treatment responses.

One investigation found that people carrying genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's responded differently to menopause hormone therapy (MHT) compared with those without the same genetic risks. The effects also varied according to the particular combination of hormones used. These findings suggest that both genetic background and hormone therapy formulation deserve consideration when evaluating treatment options. (Mateja Perović, University of Toronto).

A separate study examined rodents undergoing menopause that also carried genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's. Researchers observed that brain circuits responsible for memory became particularly vulnerable, providing evidence that menopause may represent an key period of increased susceptibility for women who are genetically predisposed to the disease. (Stephanie M. Perez, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio).

Sex Differences in Chronic Pain and Brain Inflammation.

The other two studies explored how biological sex influences pain sensitivity, immune activity, and the effects of inflammation on the brain.

In a recent development, in a mouse model of fibromyalgia, females continued to show heightened sensitivity to touch and stronger immune system activation compared with males. The findings suggest that the biological processes contributing to chronic pain may differ between sexes, potentially making treatments tailored to these differences more effective. (Yasmin Sahlloul, University of Cincinnati).

Another investigation uncovered differences in how prolonged intestinal inflammation influences the brain. Using a mouse model, researchers found that chronic gut inflammation affected brain function and Alzheimer's related disease changes differently in males and females. The results provide additional evidence that biological sex may influence the relationship between inflammation and neurological disease. (Nurcan Kilic, University of North Dakota).

Toward More Personalized Treatments for Brain Disorders.

Together, the four studies underscore the importance of examining sex and genetic differences when investigating neurological conditions. By identifying biological factors that influence disease progression and treatment responses, researchers hope to move toward more precise therapies for Alzheimer's, fibromyalgia, and other difficult-to-treat brain disorders.

In a recent development, "These four studies illustrate the fascinating discoveries that can be made when focusing on female-specific biology or possible sex differences in AD-related symptoms and risk factors," said Liisa Galea, PhD, Treliving Family Chair in Women's Mental Health at Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and moderator of the press conference. "The research presented at Neuroscience 2026 helps us pinpoint the specific differences that may help us develop more targeted treatment using precision approaches, even for some of our most complex brain disorders.".

#47721. Could an ancient solar eclipse rewrite Egyptian history?

Could an ancient solar eclipse rewrite Egyptian history?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1020 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the solar system is a clock that can be run in both directions.
  • We know when it will happen because we can calculate the motions of Earth and the moon centuries in advance.
  • Sources indicate that astronomers can reconstruct where the moon's shadow fell thousands of years ago, even when nobody left a record of it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the solar system is a clock that can be run in both directions. On Aug. 2, 2027, that clock will bring the moon's dark central shadow — a path of totality — back to Egypt. A total solar eclipse will sweep across the country, passing directly over Luxor and plunging some of ancient Egypt's greatest surviving monuments into darkness. Totality will begin in Luxor at approximately 1:02 p.m. EEST and last 6 minutes 22 seconds, according to Time and Date.

We know when it will happen because we can calculate the motions of Earth and the moon centuries in advance. But run the same celestial clock backward and eclipses become one of nature's most precise timestamps.

Sources indicate that astronomers can reconstruct where the moon's shadow fell thousands of years ago, even when nobody left a record of it. When an ancient text reliably describes an eclipse, it can anchor a moment in history to a specific place and time.

We know from astronomical calculations that eclipses crossed Egypt long before anyone left an identifiable written record of one. On April 1, 2471 B.C., a total solar eclipse swept across northern Egypt during the age of the great pyramid builders. In research published in 2025, archaeoastronomer Giulio Magli at the Polytechnic University of Milan proposed that the eclipse may help explain why Pharaoh Shepseskaf broke with tradition and built a huge rectangular tomb at South Saqqara instead of a pyramid. It's a tantalizing hypothesis, but no surviving Egyptian text records the eclipse.

Astronomers can calculate that an eclipse happened, but using it as a historical timestamp requires evidence that someone actually saw it and recorded it. That's where an eclipse almost 1,300 years later becomes particularly intriguing.

It has been revealed that A passage in the Old Testament book of Joshua describes the sun and moon as if they stopped in the sky. After leading the people of Israel into Canaan — modern-day Israel and Palestine — Joshua prayed: "Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon. And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped, until the nation took vengeance on their enemies." Ancient Gibeon is about six miles (10 kilometers) northwest of Jerusalem.

Recent findings suggest that in research published in 2017, researchers Colin Humphreys and Graeme Waddington at Cambridge University in the U.K. claimed it could refer to an annular solar eclipse on Oct. 30, 1207 B.C. It's a controversial interpretation, not least because it depends on exactly how the ancient Hebrew text is translated. However, if correct, it could be the oldest recorded solar eclipse with a date that has been identified — and it could also more accurately date the reign of Ramesses II. Also known as Ramesses the Great, he reigned for 66 years during Egypt's Fresh Kingdom, commissioned Abu Simbel, made major additions to Karnak and Luxor Temple, and lived to be over 90. His reign marked the final peak of ancient Egyptian imperial power. According to the BBC, he is the "Jupiter" of the pharaonic system. However, the precise dates of his reign remain subject to debate, with historians using a combination of archaeological, historical and astronomical evidence to reconstruct the chronology.

In a recent development, now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, the Merneptah Stele is a large inscribed granite monument written in the fifth year of Pharaoh Merneptah's reign, successor to Ramesses II. Discovered in 1896 at Merneptah's mortuary temple on the west bank of the Nile, opposite modern-day Luxor, it describes an Egyptian military campaign in Canaan and mentions Israelites. Egyptologists generally date Merneptah's reign to around 1213 — 1203 B.C., placing his fifth year around 1209/1208 B.C. That means the Israelites were already living in Canaan by then.

Recent findings suggest that using calculations that accounted for changes in Earth's rotation over thousands of years, Humphreys and Waddington identified an annular eclipse visible from Canaan for five minutes on the afternoon of Oct. 30, 1207 B.C. If the biblical passage does describe this event, that's a fixed astronomical date that could be used to refine the chronology of the Egyptian pharaohs. The researchers proposed that it occurred during the second, third or fourth year of Merneptah's reign.

It has been revealed that if Humphreys and Waddington's interpretation of the biblical text is correct, the eclipse of 1207 B.C. could be the oldest solar eclipse identified in a written record. The researchers propose that Ramesses II reigned from approximately 1276 to 1210, with an uncertainty of about a year, slightly different from the conventional dates of 1279-1213 B.C. used by the British Museum.

It has been revealed that so an eclipse can be like a timestamp on an undated photograph, but this one does not show that the book of Joshua actually describes an eclipse. The interpretation of the Hebrew has been challenged by Marinus Anthony van der Sluijs, whose paper argues that the biblical narrative states that the sun was standing over Gibeon and the moon was over the Valley of Aijalon simultaneously — so not an eclipse at all.

On Aug. 2, 2027, there will be no such ambiguity. We already know where the moon's shadow will cross Egypt, when it will reach Luxor and how long darkness will last. Almost 4,500 years separate that eclipse from the one that crossed Egypt in 2471 B.C. and 3,233 years from 1207 B.C., but both are movements of the same celestial clock. Run it forwards, and it predicts the future. Run it backward, and occasionally an eclipse of the sun can put a date on history.

He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

It has been revealed that china Renaissance stated in late February that it had learned Bao was “cooperating in an investigation” being carried out by certain authorities in the country. It gave no other details.

Missing Chinese billionaire CEO assisting authorities in investigation, firm indicates.

Industry observers note that bao is known as a veteran dealmaker who works closely with top technology companies in China. His team has also invested in US-listed Chinese electric vehicle makers Nio (NIO) and Li Auto and helped Chinese internet giants Baidu (BIDU) and JD.com (JD) complete their secondary listings in Hong Kong.

Over the weekend, China’s top anti-graft watchdog launched an investigation into Liu Liange, former party secretary and chairman of Bank of China, according to a statement by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and the State Supervision Commission. The bank is state-owned and one of the country’s four biggest lenders.

Liu is suspected of “serious violations of discipline and law,” the statement remarked. He is among the most senior financial executives targeted in a broader financial crackdown by President Xi Jinping.

In January, Wang Bin, former party chief and chairman of China Life Insurance, was charged by national-level prosecutors with taking bribes and hiding overseas savings.

Measles in America: Here's a constructive approach to beating the disease, based on Brazil's experience

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, health experts saw it coming — the fact that after 26 years, the US would lose its status as measles-free.
  • In a recent development, four months later, it was official.
  • Look at Brazil, where in 2019, with more than 21,000 measles cases, the country also lost its measles-free status.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, health experts saw it coming — the fact that after 26 years, the US would lose its status as measles-free. Back in July 2026, DW reported how one epidemiologist had suggested an 'amnesia' about the measles risk was pushing a growth in US infections.

In a recent development, four months later, it was official. On November 17, 2026, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) stated the US had lost its measles elimination status, along with Mexico.

But it doesn't have to stay this way.

Look at Brazil, where in 2019, with more than 21,000 measles cases, the country also lost its measles-free status. But within five years — during the COVID-19 pandemic — it fought and won back its measles-free status. And since 2024, Brazil has stayed measles-free, even as the highly contagious disease spread across the rest of the Americas.

In a recent development, in 2026, with the data available up to the time of writing this article, Brazil had only had 70 measles cases. They were all linked to infections brought in from abroad, often from neighboring Peru.

Brazil has fewer people than the US, about 213 million compared to the US's nearly 350 million, but the two countries are similar in size. So the comparison is worth considering.

It has been revealed that brazil moves fast. The PAHO asks countries to respond within 72 hours of a suspected measles case. Here's Brazil's own rule:.

According to recent reports, it has also made hunting for cases a national habit. In a program called "Dia S," health workers knock on doors and visit schools, daycare centers and churches to find people who may be sick but have not seen a doctor.

Brazil also holds mass vaccination days called "Dia D." There was one in November, in the area where Brazil borders Colombia and Peru.

If someone is diagnosed with measles, health workers try to track down every person the patient may have met ("contact persons") and vaccinate them and other people living nearby.

The country has so far provided more than 16 million doses of the measles vaccine in 2026 and has donated 500,000 doses to Peru.

Recent findings suggest that brazil isn't perfect, though. According to official estimates from the World Health Organization, only 76% of children got both required doses of the vaccine in 2025 — well short of the 95% target. Experts warn this leaves the country at risk because measles is so highly contagious. A country needs to be as close to 100% immunized as possible to protect people and stop the disease from spreading.

Recent findings suggest that "Elimination is not a trophy that we win once and put on a shelf. It must be protected every day," says PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The US lost its measles-free status because the PAHO found that the same strain of the virus had been spreading in the country for 12 months or more. Mexico and Bolivia lost their status on the same day as the US.

According to recent reports, the US has had more than 5,400 cases in 2026 (at time of writing), more than twice as many as in all of 2025, and about 19 times as many as in 2024. Nearly everyone who got sick with measles was unvaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status.

US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on new vaccination recommendations for children in August 2026. It came at a time, when, as we reported, experts said people had stopped getting vaccinated against measles because infection rates were low. But like PAHO's Barbosa said, neglecting vaccination when infection rates are low is a mistake.

According to recent reports, to be fair, Trump's executive order listed the measles vaccine in a top category of vaccinations recommended for every child. But the administration's stance on vaccination in general is unclear.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has often declared opposition to vaccination, including against measles, advising people to take vitamin A instead. In Texas, this led to children being hospitalized with toxic levels of the supplement, and left them with no protection against measles.

It has been revealed that before the COVID-19 pandemic, 95% of US kindergartners had their measles shots. Now, it's 92%, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Protection (CDC). That leaves about 280,000 kindergartners in the US unprotected.

In the Texas counties where a 2025 measles outbreak began, coverage was as low as 77% at the time.

US children usually need vaccines to start school, but most states let parents opt out for religious or personal reasons, with no doctor involved.

But vaccination rates have fallen elsewhere in the world as well, including in Europe. In Germany, where measles infections have also risen, experts blame anti-vaccination rhetoric that emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic.

In a recent development, A person sick with measles can infect up to18 other, unprotected people. With vaccination, it is possible to increase the number of protected people and lower the number of people the sick person can infect.

According to recent reports, to prevent a measles outbreak, a community needs about 95% of people to be vaccinated and/or immune. The vaccination consists of two doses of the MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) vaccine.

But even after the two doses, a person can expect to have only 97% protection against measles — 3% short of full protection — so, nearly everyone in the community has to be vaccinated to keep the average level of protect as close to 100% as possible.

"For some diseases like measles, even a small decrease in vaccination rates can lead to more outbreaks of disease [so] community immunity requires over 95% of susceptible individuals to be immunized," says Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics.

According to recent reports, and the 95% has to hold everywhere. A good national average can be affected by, for example, a single school where only 70% of the children are vaccinated. And that is where the outbreak is likely to start.

Around the world, measles deaths have dropped by 88% since 2000, thanks to vaccines.

But progress has stalled. Only about three out of four children worldwide get both doses of the vaccine. The biggest outbreaks right now are in Bangladesh, Indonesia and Guatemala.

Data from Europe reveals that things can get better. In the European Union, cases fell from more than 35,000 in 2024 to about 2,300 the following year, with no measles-related deaths.

Romania went from more than 30,000 cases in 2024 to about 4,200 in 2025.

In Hungary, where 99% of children are vaccinated, there have been no measles cases in the past year.

But in January, six European countries lost their measles-free status, including the UK, Spain and Austria. Across Europe, eight out of ten people who got measles in 2025 were unvaccinated.

Industry observers note that the Americas are seeing a major surge in measles infections, with more than 58,000 cases in 2026, over four times as many as by November in 2025. Guatemala has been hit hardest, with almost 35,000 cases.

The deadliest outbreaks are in Africa. African Union countries have so far reported nearly 1,800 measles deaths in 2026, about 1,650 of them in Democratic Republic of Congo. Yet, Sudan, despite the war, raised first-dose measles coverage by 22 percentage points in 2025, which was the world's largest gain.

Recent findings suggest that measles is extremely contagious. One person can infect up to 18 unprotected people, which makes it about 12 times more contagious than the flu.

In a recent development, the virus can linger in the air for up to two hours after a sick person has left the room. And people spread it before they know they are sick. Someone with measles is contagious for four days before the rash appears and four days after.

It's not just a rash. About one in five unvaccinated people who get measles in the US ends up in the hospital. Measles can weaken the immune system for years, making it harder to fight off other infections.

Sources indicate that but it's preventable. Two doses of the MMR vaccine (which also protects against mumps and rubella) protect 97% of people for life.

125,000 years ago, hippos roamed what is now the vast Arabian Desert

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1174 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A remarkable archaeological discovery in southern Saudi Arabia is revealing what life was like 125,000 years ago, when parts of the Arabian Peninsula were covered in lakes, grasslands, and thriving wildlife.
  • The discoveries come from Uruq al-Julaybah, an ancient lakeside site in the Mundafan region.
  • A Lost Green Arabia Filled With Lakes and Wildlife.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A remarkable archaeological discovery in southern Saudi Arabia is revealing what life was like 125,000 years ago, when parts of the Arabian Peninsula were covered in lakes, grasslands, and thriving wildlife. Researchers have uncovered ancient stone tools, fossils of large animals, and rare plant remains that offer an unusually detailed look at how early humans survived in this dramatically different environment.

The discoveries come from Uruq al-Julaybah, an ancient lakeside site in the Mundafan region. Announced by the Saudi Heritage Commission, the findings are the result of a joint investigation involving the Commission, King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), and Griffith University. Published in Science, the research brings together specialists in geology, archaeology, botany, and micropaleontology, along with experts from several international institutions. Their work provides notable latest evidence about prehistoric human activity, environmental change, and early human presence across the Arabian Peninsula.

A Lost Green Arabia Filled With Lakes and Wildlife.

Sources indicate that today, much of this region is dominated by desert, but the landscape looked very different during the last Interglacial period, around 125,000 years ago. This warm, humid chapter of Arabian history is often called Green Arabia, a time when plentiful water and vegetation supported large animals and human populations.

It has been revealed that using satellite-based terrain modeling, scientists reconstructed an enormous ancient lake covering approximately 340 square kilometers. The lake reached depths of up to 29 meters. Evidence from sediments, the surrounding landscape, and the remains of aquatic organisms indicates that it was a relatively stable freshwater environment bordered by open grasslands and vegetation.

The researchers identified more than 500 plant and animal fossil specimens, including invertebrates, spread across more than 130 locations. Among the animals that once inhabited the area were hippos, extinct long-horned buffaloes, camels, Arabian oryx, gazelles, and ostriches. These discoveries reveal a rich prehistoric ecosystem that bears little resemblance to the dry landscape found there today.

Thousands of Ancient Stone Tools Reveal Human Ingenuity.

Alongside the fossils, archaeologists recovered 5,511 stone tools measuring more than 2 centimeters from the main excavation area. More than 98% were made from flint, and analysis showed that the people who created them used Levallois techniques, a method of shaping stone to produce carefully prepared flakes.

Industry observers note that to better understand how the tools were made and used, researchers conducted systematic surveys using a grid system to document and collect artifacts and fossils. They also applied two dating methods to sand and fossil teeth, used three-dimensional techniques to determine how stone fragments fit together, and examined tool surfaces with microscopic and chemical analyses.

According to recent reports, these investigations uncovered intriguing evidence of how early humans used the plants around them. Residues preserved on stone tools included traces from several types of vegetation, some of which contain toxic compounds. Resin and woody material suggest that certain stone tips were attached to handles or shafts to make hunting weapons.

Sources indicate that other plant residues point to the processing of tubers, bushes, and palm leaves. This suggests that the people living around the lake relied on vegetation for a variety of purposes, from obtaining food to carrying out everyday activities.

Industry observers note that perhaps most surprisingly, the findings raise the possibility that prehistoric hunters incorporated poisonous plant compounds into their hunting technology. Although this interpretation remains tentative, it represents some of the earliest potential evidence of such practices identified in Saudi Arabia. The discoveries also include some of the region's earliest known evidence of palm-related vegetation.

A Rare Glimpse Into Everyday Life 125,000 Years Ago.

According to recent reports, what makes Uruq al-Julaybah especially valuable is the unusual combination of discoveries preserved at one location. The animal fossils, manufactured tools, and plant remains were all recovered from the same dated archaeological setting (animal remains, stone tools, and plant material), allowing scientists to piece together a remarkably complete picture of prehistoric life.

The shores of ancient Lake Mundafan appear to have provided an ideal gathering place for early humans. Freshwater, animals, vegetation, and materials suitable for making tools were all available in the surrounding landscape.

Evidence suggests that people used this environment for numerous activities, including manufacturing stone tools, preparing hunting equipment, processing animals and plants, and working with plant fibers. Taken together, the discoveries indicate that these early populations were highly adaptable and made sophisticated use of the resources available to them.

"It is very exciting to see how the collaboration of so many different specialists allows to reconstruct this uniquely complete picture of life, behavior and the environment in the distant past," said Professor Frans van Buchem, KAUST Professor of Geology and co-lead scientist.

Dr. Faisal Al-Jibreen, a Heritage Commission researcher and professor of Paleolithic archaeology who participated in the project, emphasized the importance of the discovery at Lake Mundafan in the Empty Quarter. He described it as a significant archaeological find that helps explain how the ancient environment shaped the lives of humans and animals in southern Saudi Arabia during early prehistory.

Reconstructing a Forgotten Chapter of Human History.

It has been revealed that "This site gives us a rare and richly detailed view of how people lived in a landscape that looks nothing like Arabia today," stated Professor Chris Clarkson, co-lead scientist and Professor of Archaeology at Griffith University's Australian Research Centre for Human Evolution. "The combination of animal remains, stone tools and plant material in a single, dated context is what makes this discovery so significant.".

By bringing together different kinds of archaeological and environmental evidence, the researchers have reconstructed a period of Arabian history that is difficult to imagine from the region's present-day appearance. Their findings offer key clues about how early humans moved across the Arabian Peninsula, developed technology, and adapted their behavior to changing environmental conditions.

According to recent reports, "Saudi Arabia has an exceptional archaeological heritage. Building Heritage Science capabilities in the Kingdom will enable us to turn the smallest traces into the biggest stories," remarked Professor Laurence Hapiot, co-author and Head of Heritage Research at KAUST.

The investigation reflects an extensive international research effort to better understand the Arabian Peninsula's ancient human and environmental history. The Saudi Heritage Commission supported fieldwork during the 2023 season, helped fund the research, and facilitated scientific activities.

Along with KAUST, Griffith University in Australia, and King Saud University, the project involved international universities and research centers specializing in archaeology, ancient environments, history, and laboratory analysis. This collaboration demonstrates how combining expertise from different scientific fields can uncover extraordinary details about human life thousands of generations in the past.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that NASA has introduced a $1 million Moon Base Challenge, inviting teams of students from high schools and colleges across the United States to help develop ideas for humanity's future on the Moon. The competition was announced during a MAX POWER event at Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida. Presented as part of a Golden Age of Science, the initiative gives young innovators an opportunity to contribute designs and potential solutions for NASA's planned lunar base.

"We're looking for students ready to think creatively, work as a team, and take on real problems connected to NASA's future on the Moon," said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. "You do not have to wait until graduation to contribute. Curiosity, creativity, and the willingness to tackle hard problems without obvious answers are exactly the qualities we need as we build what comes next.".

NASA's Intends for a Permanent Moon Base.

Industry observers note that NASA is working toward establishing a Moon Base near the lunar South Pole, where astronauts will be able to live, conduct research, and explore the surrounding region. Creating a lasting human presence on the Moon is also an important step toward future missions that will carry astronauts to Mars. Achieving these goals will require expertise and creative thinking from people across a wide range of industries and disciplines.

According to recent reports, "As we build and design the foundations of Moon Base, we want to leverage all the ingenuity and innovation to think of every consideration our explorers might need to live and work there," remarked Carlos García-Galán, manager, Moon Base Program. "Students bring exactly the bold ideas that we're looking for, and I'm looking forward to their fresh perspective. Ultimately, Moon Base is for them, people who will experience a world where humans are on the Moon to stay.".

Six Major Challenges of Living on the Moon.

It has been revealed that the competition will unfold in multiple phases, with student teams developing solutions to six essential aspects of operating a lunar base. These include generating and storing power, constructing facilities, maintaining life support systems, enabling transportation across the lunar surface, establishing communications networks, and protecting astronauts.

Each category addresses practical obstacles that NASA must overcome to support long-term operations on the Moon. By working on these problems, students can explore new approaches to lunar technologies while developing technical and professional skills that could prepare them for careers in aerospace and related fields.

In a recent development, the challenge is designed around actual environmental conditions and mission requirements that would affect daily life and operations on the lunar surface. Participants will produce work similar to that used in the space industry, including evaluations of competing technical options, proposals outlining potential designs, and presentations for project stakeholders.

In a recent development, students from technical, vocational, and other academic backgrounds are encouraged to participate. Previous specialized knowledge of engineering or related technical fields is not required, making the competition accessible to a broad range of young innovators.

Inspiring the Next Generation of Space Explorers.

Beyond generating ideas for the Moon Base, NASA hopes the competition will help develop the skills needed by the next generation of aerospace professionals. By exposing students to practical design challenges, the agency aims to encourage collaboration, creative problem-solving, and greater involvement in future space exploration.

According to recent reports, "Students are the next generation of explorers and innovators. Their unique perspectives are key to helping us envision a future away from Earth, and I'm excited to see the creativity and ingenuity spurred by this challenge," remarked Elaine Ho, associate administrator for the Office of STEM Engagement at NASA Headquarters.

How to Enter NASA's $1 Million Moon Base Challenge.

In a recent development, interested student teams must register through the NASA STEM Gateway. Registration remains open until January 25, 2027.

NASA's Office of STEM Engagement developed the competition in partnership with the agency's Moon Base Program. The Institute of Competition Sciences is responsible for administering the challenge under a contract with NASA's Center of Excellence for Collaborative Innovation, which operates within the Research and Technology Mission Directorate.

Breaking: The Smart Ring Goes to Church

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1355 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, stressed?
  • According to recent reports, the first generation of Christian smart rings is here, joining other religious wearables like iQibla’s dedicated Muslim smartwatches, rings, and Hajj bands alongside “kosher” smartwatch apps.
  • Everblessed’s $249 Elah Ring S1 went on sale in October and is shipping in the US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, stressed? Heart rate elevated? If you’re wearing a smart ring from Oura, Ultrahuman, or Samsung, the spike could prompt app suggestions like breathing exercises, meditations, or a physical reset like a short walk. So far, so Silicon Valley. But now you can add reading the Bible to that list of self-soothing activities.

According to recent reports, the first generation of Christian smart rings is here, joining other religious wearables like iQibla’s dedicated Muslim smartwatches, rings, and Hajj bands alongside “kosher” smartwatch apps. Two new devices in particular—Glorify’s Ring and Everblessed Technology’s Elah Ring—connect to hugely popular Christian prayer apps with tens of millions of people, and both claim to be the world’s first Christian smart ring.

Both are first, in their own ways. Everblessed’s $249 Elah Ring S1 went on sale in October and is shipping in the US. The $299 Glorify Ring debuted in July, with reservations open and shipping set for January 2027, but 77,000 units of an earlier beta iteration, the Amen Ring made by faith tech firm ConfideIn (which merged with Glorify this May), were given away last Christmas. Everblessed manages the Blessed app, and Glorify has an eponymous app.

Another big player in prayer apps is Hallow, aimed at Catholics, backed by Vice President JD Vance’s Narya venture capital firm and celebrity ambassadors, with 24 million installs to date. Hallow’s toe-dip into wearables was a 2024 smart rosary with NFC embedded in the crucifix, made with Italian brand Ghirelli; Everblessed tried an earbud, necklace, and bedside device before settling on the ring design.

Head-to-head on design, the Elah and Glorify rings are both made from titanium alloy, with a thorn-inspired twist for Glorify and a minimalist band featuring a cross for the Elah S1, which is also IP68 waterproof to 5 meters.

Recent findings suggest that for now, the Elah Ring is slightly techier: prayer reminders come via the cross, which glows via an LED, and “gentle” vibrations; these can pulse at certain times of day or be triggered by changes in heart rate and stress levels, picked up by a photoplethysmography (PPG) sensor. Glorify’s CEO Henry Costa tells WIRED these emotion-based reminders will land on the Glorify Ring in six months; for now, you can set the times of day you want prayer reminders, track heart rate, blood oxygen, stress, and sleep via the optical sensor.

One addition to the Glorify Ring that Costa indicates he personally uses “a lot” is recording prayers straight into the built-in mic. The ring has a light to signal when it's recording, and the app transcribes them. Everblessed CEO Ricky Xia says that, after consulting with pastors and users, the feeling was that voice notes on the ring were seen as “suspicious.” It’s available in-app, but most people don’t pray out loud, and too many features drain the battery life. (The Elah Ring runs for up to six days on one charge; Glorify for four to five days.).

In a recent development, both companies see the smart ring nudges helping wearers prioritize meaningful quiet time, away from screens, while offering in-app Christian practices as an alternative to Eastern meditation. Glorify offers Bible study, courses, and meditations. Blessed has devotional “anchors,” Bible texts and audio, plus guided breathing. Xia indicates he’s happy if the Elah vibrates and a user picks up a paper Bible rather than the Blessed app, while Costa says he’s “crying out to use my phone less.”.

In a recent development, both Glorify (founded in 2020, now merged with ConfideIn and headquartered in the San Francisco Bay Area) and Blessed (founded in 2023 and based in San Jose) operate in more than 150 countries. Perhaps the biggest difference between the two rings is their relationship to AI.

Xia is all-in, describing the S1 as an “AI-native” product, with a pastor-complementing, not-replacing FaithMate chatbot in the Blessed app, customized based on preferences, congregation, and depth of learning. ChatGPT is like a “good coworker,” he states, while FaithMate is designed to be “your friend” and an agent that can also handle secular tasks.

“A lot of our users not only ask questions about the Bible but also ask about themselves, their relationships with their wives, they’re being bullied at school," Xia says, stressing safeguards around data storage, encryption, and privacy. "Everyone is going to have some AI that they trust, and how they view that is built on their personal stuff, their private vulnerabilities.”.

Industry observers note that costa is more circumspect, treading carefully on the consumer-facing side and noting that the Pope has weighed in with a 6,000-word encyclical on AI. A launch interview with CBN News garnered negative comments: “AI is Antichrist Information,” for one.

Recent findings suggest that “The stance I’ve always taken is that our daily devotional is hand-authored by a team of theologians,” Costa states. “It’s prayed over, and that is a stamp of approval.” He criticizes AI slop prayer apps as inauthentic. Still, he says the Glorify team has already tested “many forms” of AI personalization: “Any time, if we do use AI, it must be very clear to the user.”.

Smart ring owners were finding ways to add faith features to mainstream accessories before these rings came to fruition. For 20 years, timer and reminder apps have helped with prayer schedules, but recent examples are more creative. Heidi Campbell, professor of communication in religious studies at Texas A&M, refers to these DIY upgrades to the Oura ring and devices like the Muse headband as “spiritual mind-body hacking.”.

Oura owners on #christiantiktok chat about how they already use the ring’s stress and HR alerts as a prompt to pause and reflect, as per Elah.

Recent findings suggest that smart ring consumers flag changes in resting heart rate and sleep quality with scripture following their daily practice. “It’s really helpful for, like, what was inhibiting me from getting to a meditative or contemplative prayer state?” Campbell states. “It takes some of the mystery out of prayer, I think, but that can also be positive. There is a way to do prayer well and not well.” Ring hackers can also dig into health stats during Lent, Ramadan, and Yom Kippur to analyze energy expenditure and how fasting periods affect their bodies.

AI-powered voice recordings and emerging attempts at emotion tracking are part of a latest phase for smart rings, says Ekta Mittal, a senior analyst of connected devices at CCS Insight. These new “purpose-driven” features extend wearable tech into “new parts of consumers’ daily routines,” Mittal says. She suggests that while Glorify and Everblessed will add value for some, the rings are “not directly competing” with established smart ring giants like Oura, Ultrahuman, and Samsung.

Industry observers note that the pandemic sped up the digital transition of many places of worship when congregations could not meet up in person, encouraging experimentation with social media. So it’s early days for Silicon Valley’s impact on organized religion. Researchers at the University of Würzburg in Germany, led by Ilona Nord, are studying the theological implications of using tech, including smart rings, for spiritual practices, investigating which values are baked into secular devices and apps.

Campbell suggests many Christian groups haven’t stopped to consider the unintentional consequences of cultivating spirituality via personal tech. “All of these things are about individualizing the practice, which is good, but the challenges are for religions which are really focused on communal aspects,” she states. Not everyone has the money or connectivity to access these gadgets, but also, more existentially, “it puts spiritual development over communal development.”.

It has been revealed that xia points to the Blessed app’s communities, including its Healing Room broadcast feature, which lets pastors go live with sermons. It's not in the Elah app yet, but it's on the roadmap. Costa says communal practice is a core pillar, highlighting the “social layer” of public notes made on Christian texts in-app and an upcoming Glorify Ring feature which will allow a user to pair their device with a family member’s ring: “When your loved one is feeling down, you’ll get a buzz to check in with them.”.

It has been revealed that if three seasons of Yellowjackets has taught us anything, it's that you don't mess with Shauna Shipman (aka Shauna Sadecki). Melissa learned that the hard way last season, when she sent a tape that put the Yellowjackets on her scent.

Shauna (Melanie Lynskey) didn't just find her, attack her, and bite off a bit of Melissa's arm. She also tried to feed it to her. Well, Season 4 of Yellowjackets came back with a vengeance, and so did Melissa (Hillary Swank).

Fresh from killing Van (Lauren Ambrose), Melissa begins episode 1 on the run with her wife, Alex (Jaylee Hamidi), and their child. In a grimy hotel room, she confesses to her partner the truth (or some of it). Her name is not Kelly, it's Melissa. She was a Yellowjacket. She was on the plane that crashed.

According to recent reports, melissa says she "rebooted her life" — which is a wild way to reframe faking your death. "I'm still the same person you married," she insists, "just with a different name and way, way shittier past than I told you about on our first date.".

Then this conversation reveals something huge:.

Alex responds to Melissa's partial confession with: "My mom was out there. She's the one who called for help. She's the reason they got rescued. ".

In a recent development, so, there were signs last season about how Tai (Jasmin Savoy Brown), Van (Liv Hewson), Shauna (Sophie Nélisse), and Misty (Samantha Hanratty) talked about Hannah (Ashley Sutton) that suggested she didn't make it out of the Yellowjackets camp alive. Alex's revelation further cements that Hannah died out there. When Alex asks her wife if she met her mom out there, Melissa lies, "No. I didn't know her.".

Melissa goes on to say that it was because she wish she'd known Hannah that she moved to the late scientist's hometown to start over. "Maybe I could create a life in her honor," she says. That might be true. But even as Melissa comes clean, she's still lying to Alex. And by sharing any of this, Melissa could be putting Alex in danger from the others. At least she's honest about that.

In a recent development, the episode begins with the Yellowjackets in a Canadian hospital, seeing their injuries tended to. But there's no sign of Hannah.

As the Yellowjackets share their story of survival with authorities, they all recite the exact same story:.

It has been revealed that "The plane crashed. Our friends died. And the rest of starved and scavenged and prayed until they finally found us.".

They claim to have no knowledge of the missing frog scientists. To cover their tracks, they let the adults assume Hannah made the distress call. So, Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) never gets proper credit for her heroics there.

How Hannah died, however, is still a mystery.

After the scene of Melissa's confession to her wife, a title card says four weeks have passed. Shauna is acting out in her frustration, lashing out at a convenience store clerk and a stinky detective, the latter of whom has lost any trace of Melissa and her family.

Sources indicate that cut to: Melissa and Alex setting up in a newly leased home — which is right next door to the Sadecki household. Alex seems nervous about the strategy, as Melissa assures, "Hey, we can't run forever.".

Then, Melissa confronts Shauna by showing up at her door with a "Hi" and a bottle of wine. To this, Shauna says, "Well, this was very stupid... You moved in next door to me. Now I know where you are.".

Melissa responds, "Yeah, and everyone else will too," just as a news van pulls up behind her!

In the wilderness and in the present timeline, Melissa knows full well how Shauna's rage can result in violence, sometimes deadly violence.

However, she also knows Shauna is strategic and a survivor. By staying in plain sight, Melissa thinks Shauna will be powerless to hurt her, because to do so would bring fresh attention to the Yellowjackets and their past.

Is she right? We'll can't wait to find out.
