#47695. Tech Report: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1274 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1274 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function.
  • It has been revealed that the findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time.
  • It has been revealed that the discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.

It has been revealed that the findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.

It has been revealed that the discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.

These questions are especially important because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.

In a recent development, to investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.

More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills.

One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

Cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn new things, and solve problems. These abilities play an important role in school performance and everyday decision-making.

The findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.

"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.

"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.

Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently.

The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.

Industry observers note that among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.

Industry observers note that working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing fresh information.

Sources indicate that light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.

The differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.

Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity.

The study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.

Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.

Industry observers note that one possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.

This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.

"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.

"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is crucial to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing.".

What the Eight-Year Study Revealed.

The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.

Recent findings suggest that the current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.

Recent findings suggest that researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.

In a recent development, to evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.

Industry observers note that importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.

In a recent development, nevertheless, the results offer an important perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.

The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.

Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.

The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Khalil Roberts had heard horror stories of people getting kicked off Instagram for using third-party apps to purge follower counts, so when he came across an X post claiming that Muse—Meta’s AI assistant—could mass-unfollow people who didn’t follow him back, he didn’t believe it.

“I’ve never gone through my exact list to vet those people out, but I’ve always been curious,” the 31-year-old Newly introduced Yorker tells WIRED. But after realizing that by using Muse, his account wouldn’t get flagged as spam, his mind was made up. “I was like, I actually will be a little petty.”.

Sources indicate that after downloading Muse, Roberts, who had over 7,600 followers, entered the prompt: “Can you show me a list of people (non celebrity) that [don’t] follow me back on instagram and can you unfollow them for me. ”.

In a recent development, within minutes, Muse identified 151 accounts. It attached an Excel sheet with a breakdown of everyone cataloged—separated by categories identifying their username, real name, classification, and profile link—and asked if Roberts wanted to proceed with his request. Shockingly, some of the names were people he thought of as friends. “It was a little surprising, but also a reminder that we don’t have a relationship anymore.”.

Sources indicate that following the success of his November 7 cleanse, Roberts posted about it on X, offering instructions to his followers. Over the past several weeks, parallel scenarios have played out across X, Instagram, and Facebook, with owners sharing tips on how to automate their unfollows with the help of Muse.

X user @justdrmj posted about the trend the same week as Roberts, and nearly every reply shared a taste for trivial grudge-holding. For him it came down to one simple rule: “Why be a fan?” “i agree. reciprocity is key,” one person noted in response. “The way I just cleaned house,” added another. In a seeming outburst of celebration, one X user posted: “Just unfollowed 1000+ people on IG.”.

Even tech worker Kimberly Munoz, who has 33,200 Instagram followers, said she wasn’t about to be “anybody’s fan,” noting in an Instagram video that she used the feature to suss out “people that I know in real life that have unfollowed me.” “I downloaded Muse just to do this only,” one person responded.

Industry observers note that with social media rapidly evolving, there is no longer a unified consensus around etiquette. For some people, following others is an indication of friendship or simply a way to keep tabs on your latest crush. Others view it as more of a social obligation—you follow someone if they follow you, but the opposite is true as well.

Natalie Pennington, an associate professor who researches social connection at Colorado State University, wonders about the consequences of people gradually outsourcing small social decisions to technology.

“It is probably at least partially a question of not wanting to deal with emotionally uncomfortable things,” Pennington indicates. “This also strikes me as another example of information we don’t really need that social media can give us. There’s this data that exists at the platform level or would take a lot of effort to find out on your own, but now you can learn with the click of the button. But it doesn’t mean it is something you need to know.”.

In October, despite the seeming popularity of the feature, Meta removed an advertising campaign that promoted Muse with the promise that users could “see who unfollowed you each week,” Business Insider reported.

When WIRED asked about the reasoning behind Meta’s decision to remove the ad, the organization did not respond to a request for comment.

Industry observers note that but Muse’s capabilities aren’t just being employed to even scores. Some people are using the assistant to streamline feeds that have become extremely cluttered over the years.

Elizabeth Brooks is a self-proclaimed “sweeper”—the term for a hobbyist who routinely enters sweepstakes and promotional contests—who, over the course of 10 years, had followed various accounts offering giveaways. Recently, she started prompting the assistant to bring her five profile links every few hours, no more than six times a day, for her to manually unfollow one by one. “Your following list can finally work for you instead of the other way around,” she wrote on Facebook.

Roberts, who joined Instagram in high school 15 years ago and calls the platform “my app of choice,” claims people are becoming more intentional about their digital relationships and who they let into their online lives. But he doesn’t proposal on letting Muse make any more decisions about his social life, he says.

“Unfollowing is where I draw the line.”.

Industry observers note that graves says he does not pay celebrities to attend his events but instead provides a high-end, all-inclusive outing. “I want it to be like, ‘I want to go hang out with Todd and go to this event.’ It’s first-class, great hotels, transportation, security,” Graves says of his pitch. “No one in there wants anything from them but friendship, hanging out.”.

He adds that on top of the fact that “the dinners are great, the parties are fun, there’s DJs and performers that they like,” it’s crucial to him to take out the corporate element, with no business partners in his rooms “hitting people up or asking for selfies.”.

Graves confirms that the company measures impressions after every event, and “it’s amazing for sales,” he adds. “You see long-term loyalty because [customers] are like, ‘The person that I really love and respect loves Cane’s and actually wants to hang out with the founder.’ “.

#47690. Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (780 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (780 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism.
  • The findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal key differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).
  • The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism. Although adults with and without autism showed remarkably similar brain activity when researchers compared group averages, a closer examination uncovered striking differences between individuals. These differences were especially pronounced in brain regions involved in understanding and responding to social information.

The findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal key differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The discovery could help scientists better understand why autism varies so widely from person to person and eventually support more personalized approaches to care.

The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.

What Brain Scans Reveal When People Watch Movies.

Recent findings suggest that to explore these differences, the team examined previously collected brain imaging data from Indiana University and Caltech. The recordings captured brain activity as adults with and without autism watched movies from several genres, including animation, action, romantic comedy, and Hitchcockian thrillers.

According to recent reports, movies offered researchers a way to study how the brain responds to a constantly changing stream of sights, sounds, and social interactions. Unlike simple laboratory tasks, movies present a rich mixture of information that more closely resembles the complexity of everyday experiences.

It has been revealed that using the imaging data, the researchers trained a computational model to identify connections between brain activity and different elements of the movies. These included visual details, sounds, and more abstract social information, such as interactions between characters.

After training, the model was able to accurately predict activity across several brain systems.

Kliemann explained why this approach is particularly useful for investigating the social challenges sometimes associated with autism: "The computational model allowed us to look for robust brain responses to many different aspects of the complex, dynamic contexts in the movies.".

A Surprising Difference Hidden by Brain Activity Averages.

The most unexpected finding emerged when researchers compared the two groups.

Recent findings suggest that at first, the results suggested relatively little difference. When brain responses were averaged across participants, the model predicted activity in various brain systems similarly for adults with and without autism.

However, the picture changed when the researchers examined how much individual participants differed from others in their own group.

People with autism revealed substantially greater variation in their brain responses than participants without autism. In other words, although the overall group averages looked similar, the responses of individual autistic participants were much less alike.

According to recent reports, this increased variability appeared across nearly every brain system examined. The strongest differences occurred in the social brain system, a network of regions involved in processing social information and understanding other people.

Why the Findings Could Change Autism Research.

In a recent development, the results raise crucial questions about how scientists investigate autism. Many existing approaches to understanding and treating the condition rely heavily on comparing average measurements from groups of autistic and nonautistic individuals.

But if autistic people show considerable differences in how their brains process information, these averages may obscure some of the most meaningful findings.

Traer described the team's surprise: "We were surprised by the similarity of group averages. The results suggest that we need to focus on understanding the details of individual brain responses. How and why do they differ?".

Rather than searching only for brain activity patterns shared by everyone with autism, the findings point toward the potential value of studying individuals and identifying smaller groups with similar characteristics.

Kliemann highlighted what this could mean for future research and support: "Identifying ASD subgroups may help us build a more precise understanding of the condition and help develop ways to provide individually tailored support.".

Industry observers note that the researchers now plan to investigate how these differences in brain activity relate to variations in autism-related behavior. They hope to determine where and when the differences emerge, how they are connected to individual characteristics, and what might explain them.

Ultimately, the findings suggest that understanding autism may require looking beyond the average brain and paying closer attention to the distinctive ways individuals process the world.

#47688. GTA hasn't gone to space (yet), but these sci-fi games can offer you a life of crime among the stars

GTA hasn't gone to space (yet), but these sci-fi games can offer you a life of crime among the stars

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1300 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, GTA 6 has only just come out, and it's already taken the world by storm and positioned itself as one of the greatest games of all time.
  • According to recent reports, to this day, Rockstar Games sadly hasn't embraced sci-fi with any of its open-world games (save for those UFO Easter eggs).
  • It has been revealed that the frustrating thing is that no one has exactly cracked that pitch yet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, GTA 6 has only just come out, and it's already taken the world by storm and positioned itself as one of the greatest games of all time. Great news for gamers, but what about sci-fi fans?

According to recent reports, to this day, Rockstar Games sadly hasn't embraced sci-fi with any of its open-world games (save for those UFO Easter eggs). It doesn't seem likely they'll journey to the stars anytime soon — you can't really do cutting societal satire about space — but that doesn't mean there aren't GTA-adjacent sci-fi adventures set in outer space.

It has been revealed that the frustrating thing is that no one has exactly cracked that pitch yet. Non-linear games set in outer space tend to be either too ambitious, like No Man's Sky, or too focused on specific experiences like space combat, like Star Wars: Squadrons.

The end result is a roster of great sandboxes that let us journey to different star systems, but no game that dares to explore a criminal fantasy with the level of depth and opportunities seen in the last few Rockstar games.

With fresh hardware powering far more complex open-world games, it's only a matter of time before "GTA in space" is a real thing. For now, there are some space games that let us explore sci-fi worlds, roleplaying as criminals and outlaws amongst the stars.

Recent findings suggest that massive space RPGs like Starfield and The Outer Worlds 2 offer vast playgrounds you can explore and redefine through your actions. The lawful path is the obvious choice if you'd like to save the galaxy, but a life of crime awaits those who tire of the heroics.

Recent findings suggest that starfield even has a "newly introduced game plus" mechanic baked into the player's journey, encouraging experimentation and living different lives, so if you stick with the divisive space RPG, the criminal life is all but unavoidable. And in traditional Bethesda fashion, you're not rushed to the next "main" objective, so if you want to become the most dangerous space criminal in the Settled Systems, you'll be supported by the mechanics and systems. You can always get back to saving the galaxy when you feel like it.

The Outer Worlds 2 is another option if you want to become a star-surfing scoundrel. It might not be as absurdly expansive as Starfield, but Obsidian's whole deal has always been freedom of choice and roleplaying, so you can bet this humorous sequel also lets the protagonist become a bit of an a-hole. The main story already sets you in a collision course with corporate interests, too. Like in Mass Effect and other classic space RPGs, it's your choice to be either a goody-two-shoes or an edgy maniac, and I won't lie: the second option is usually more entertaining.

Last but not least, there's a third game that also has enough going on to support a GTA-inspired fantasy in outer space: No Man's Sky.

It has been revealed that it's grown so much over the years that its original space exploration premise has been buried by content like fully customizable space stations, actual cities and towns with alien NPCs, gigantic kaiju-like beasts, and... fishing. The endless free updates have pushed the roleplaying aspects deeper, as Hello Games are really making it the "forever" space game.

In a recent development, most importantly though, you can be the greatest bad guy the virtually infinite universe has ever seen, controlling entire pirate fleets and firing on (or stealing) every spaceship that you come across. It might be a bit aimless for some, but if you love a "forever game" then NMS can be the biggest space-set criminal sim ever created.

Though it took too long, Star Wars has gotten really close to cracking the GTA formula in outer space in a shameless enough way. 2024's Star Wars Outlaws is, to this date, the closest thing we've received to a space-set sandbox directly inspired by Rockstar's huge hits.

In a recent development, by letting us fully embrace the Han Solo-like scoundrel fantasy, Massive Entertainment delivered a Star Wars adventure that's all about breaking the law. Hell, they even got a wanted system in there that has protagonist Kay Vess dodging stormtroopers and rival criminal factions like you would in Vice City.

It has been revealed that star Wars Outlaws' take on GTA isn't just about the surface-level gameplay and open structure; it also understands much of its playful tone, moral ambiguity, and stressful rhythm. Jumping between several medium-sized maps set on different planets and spaceship sections breaks up the experience a little, so it never quite reaches that level of seamless immersion, but if anyone wants to do a focused version of GTA in space in the future, Massive's attempt is the one game that got at least halfway there.

Before we go (and before you go back to playing GTA VI), we should remember the daring video games that, for a variety of reasons, never got to realize their visions of a crime-oriented space adventure.

Remember Star Wars 1313 and Visceral Games' cancelled project? It's hard not to spot some of their DNA surviving in Outlaws. As Luke Skywalker wisely said before noping out, "No one's ever really gone." Lucasfilm loves that, and it extends to binned video games too, thankfully. Even the elusive Battlefront 3 is back from the dead now.

Bethesda also had something going at some point with "Prey 2", a bounty hunter action game set in a cyberpunk-ish alien world. Before it was canned, it dropped one of the coolest CG game trailers ever made and teased us with a Blade Runner-esque future long before Cyberpunk hit our consoles.

Recent findings suggest that looking at the future, Ubisoft's Beyond Good & Evil 2 wants to go big and lawless, potentially iterating on Star Wars Outlaws and other open-world crime sims. But years after its announcement and many mind-boggling development news updates, it's hard to believe it's really ever coming out. Maybe the "Before GTA VI" meme can morph into "Before BG&E2" now that Rockstar's masterpiece is finally out.

Ultimately, Rockstar is Rockstar. A one-of-a-kind megastudio with nearly unlimited resources. Trying to replicate GTA does — either on Earth or among the stars — would be an Icarus flight in the making for most studios. There are some GTA-flavored space adventures out there, as we've shown, but we're still waiting for the one. Something that matches the deep storytelling, complete freedom, and cheeky tone of Rockstar's iconic series. OK, I gotta get out of here, I'm too hip for this, I gotta play GTA VI some more.

Jason and Lucia have always known the deck is stacked against them. But when an easy score goes wrong, they find themselves on the darkest side of the sunniest place in America, in the middle of a criminal conspiracy stretching across the state of Leonida — forced to rely on each other more than ever if they want to make it out alive.

Fran Ruiz is our resident Star Wars guy. His hunger for movies and TV series is only matched by his love for video games. #47687. The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected

The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1170 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the way people describe their lives may offer surprising clues about their personalities, including traits associated with psychopathy.
  • Researchers examined hundreds of personal life stories and discovered that three major traits associated with psychopathy, boldness, meanness, and disinhibition, were connected to distinctly different ways of using words.
  • The findings, published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences, suggest that psychopathic traits can influence everyday communication in subtle ways that conventional stereotypes often overlook.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the way people describe their lives may offer surprising clues about their personalities, including traits associated with psychopathy. A new study from the University of Mississippi challenges the familiar image of psychopaths as cold and emotionless, revealing that their patterns of language can be far more complex than expected.

Researchers examined hundreds of personal life stories and discovered that three major traits associated with psychopathy, boldness, meanness, and disinhibition, were connected to distinctly different ways of using words. Some of the findings were particularly unexpected. For example, people who scored higher in meanness tended to use more positive language, while those with greater boldness used fewer words associated with anxiety.

The findings, published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences, suggest that psychopathic traits can influence everyday communication in subtle ways that conventional stereotypes often overlook.

It has been revealed that "The goal here is not to diagnose psychopathy based on language," mentioned Ky Bray, an Ole Miss doctoral candidate in psychology. "It's to point to the fact that psychopathy shows up in everyday behaviors, even subtle behaviors like language.

"If we want to understand psychopathy and the different traits that comprise it, we need to think creatively about how these traits shape social interaction.".

What 450 Life Stories Revealed About Psychopathy.

The researchers used a psychological framework known as the Triarchic Model of Psychopathy, which examines three distinct personality dimensions. Boldness generally involves confidence and fearlessness, meanness reflects tendencies toward callousness and reduced empathy, and disinhibition involves difficulties with impulse control. According to Laura Drislane, an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Mississippi, these characteristics can affect ordinary behaviors, including how people describe their own experiences.

To investigate these connections, Drislane and Bray recruited 450 participants, including college students and individuals who reported having been incarcerated. Each person responded to open questions about important moments in their life, including their greatest highs, lowest points, and major turning points.

After writing their personal accounts, participants completed a questionnaire designed to measure their levels of psychopathic traits. The researchers then analyzed the written responses using specialized software that identifies patterns in word choice.

The analysis focused on how frequently participants used language associated with different psychological categories, including positive and negative emotions, achievement, social influence or clout, and risk. By comparing these language patterns with the personality scores, the team identified several intriguing relationships.

Surprising Differences in Positive and Negative Language.

Participants with higher disinhibition scores generally used more negative words in their personal stories. They were also less likely to mention friends or use language connected to positive emotions and personal achievement.

According to recent reports, meanness, however, demonstrated a very different pattern. People scoring higher in this trait tended to use more positive language, along with more words related to achievement and rewards. They also used fewer expressions associated with negative emotions.

Boldness was associated with another distinctive pattern. Participants with higher scores used fewer anxiety-related words, including terms such as fear, afraid, and worry. Their personal accounts also contained fewer references to mental illness.

Industry observers note that these differences suggest that psychopathic traits do not produce a single recognizable style of communication. Instead, different characteristics are associated with different ways of describing emotions, goals, relationships, and personal experiences.

"What this tells us is the story we tell about our life has meaning," Drislane stated. "It helps people make sense of their experiences, develop a worldview and a coherent sense of who they are.

"What we're starting to see is that in psychopathy, there are traits that relate to differences in meaning-making and the ways people think about their life.".

Why Psychopathy Is More Complex Than the Stereotypes.

The researchers also discovered that the relationship between personality traits and language changed depending on which question participants were answering. Someone describing a difficult experience, for example, might use language differently than when recalling a personal success.

According to recent reports, this variation is crucial because it challenges the assumption that psychopathy is characterized by consistently flat or emotionally empty communication. Instead, the findings indicate that language patterns depend on both the particular psychopathic trait and the context in which someone is telling their story.

"People tend to think of psychopathy as one thing, but it's actually multidimensional," Bray stated. "What we mean when we say that everyone exists on this spectrum. Everyone has some degree of meanness, boldness, and disinhibition.

"Viewing it from a multidimensional perspective allows us to observe how those traits might manifest in nonforensic populations, in people who have not committed a crime. That allows us to see how these traits affect college students, business professionals, or interpersonal relationships.".

It has been revealed that like many personality conditions, psychopathy is better understood as a spectrum rather than a simple distinction between people who have it and those who do not. At one extreme is the familiar cultural image of a "psychopath," while people at the opposite end score low in all three dimensions.

Sources indicate that this approach allows researchers to examine psychopathic traits throughout the general population, including among people who have never committed a crime. It also helps explain why the same broad label can encompass individuals with very different personalities and behaviors.

How Understanding Psychopathic Traits Could Improve Treatment.

Recognizing these differences has implications beyond understanding everyday speech. Researchers have linked dimensions of psychopathy to serious outcomes, including criminal behavior, repeat offending, and intimate partner violence. Examining each trait separately may provide a clearer picture of how these risks develop.

It has been revealed that "That's in part why there's a movement away from calling people 'psychopaths,' because we don't view psychopathy as a category," Drislane said. "But psychopathic dimensions can predict important outcomes, things like crime, recidivism, or intimate partner violence.

"What our research, including this paper, suggests is that it's important to look beyond that label and into the different components or dimensions of psychopathy, because each of those dimensions actually has a unique set of outcomes or things that it can predict.".

Industry observers note that researchers also emphasize that psychopathy can be treated, with interventions aimed at reducing problematic symptoms and behaviors. Understanding the psychological processes behind boldness, meanness, and disinhibition could help scientists develop more targeted approaches and potentially identify ways to prevent severe problems from emerging.

Sources indicate that "If we want to be able to treat or ideally even prevent psychopathy from developing, we need to understand the mechanisms at play," she stated. "That comes down to understanding the unique contributors for all three of these dimensions.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stephan James has played a few real-life figures in his career, including Olympic gold medalist Jesse Owens (in 2016’s “Race”) and civil rights leader John Lewis (2014’s “Selma”), so he knows the drill. Diving deep into the archives for research. Vocal coaching. Perhaps a physical transformation.

His mission: honor the man, the mythic character he originated and their combined legacy. (Weathers died in 2024 at 76.) “It’s not lost on me, just how crucial Carl Weathers was not only in this franchise, but what he represented as a young Black leading man during that era,” James tells Variety, sitting down for an extensive interview about the role. “So, I just wanted to do that person justice and give him as many colors as I could in the short amount of time that I had in this film.”.

Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky,” now playing in theaters nationwide, focuses on the unbelievable true story of how Sylvester Stallone (portrayed by Anthony Ippolito) came to write “Rocky” and ultimately play the title role. But as much as the movie focuses on Stallone’s star-making moment, it also spotlights the key casting of Weathers, a former pro football star, who’d played bit parts on demonstrates like “Good Times,” “The Six Million Dollar Man” and “Kung Fu.”.

James shines in the character’s introduction scene: a crackling sequence in which Weathers auditions to play Apollo Creed, the heavyweight champ whom Stallone’s underdog Rocky will fight. James’ Weathers struts in with his shirt unbuttoned to reveal impressively toned abs. When the casting director asks his age, he quips: “Honey, I’m young as the sun and old as spit. Whatever, you need me to be.” It’s all going swimmingly — he delivers his lines with panache; he’s got experience in the boxing ring (a fib, but we’ll get to that later) — until it’s time to read with a mumbling Stallone.

“Look, can we cut?” Weathers says, leaping to his feet to complain about his scene partner. “I would really do better if I had a real actor reading with me, goddamnit.” When he’s informed that Stallone is the writer and lead actor of the picture, he replies, slyly: “Well maybe he’ll get better.”.

The fine-tuned comedy is a different look for the 32-year-old Canadian star, best known for dramatic parts — like “If Beale Street Could Talk,” “Homecoming,” “The Piano Lesson” and “Ricky” — and he plays it all with a mischievous glint in his eye.

“He’s got so much presence. He’s so magnetic that it wasn’t hard,” James indicates about filming the sequence. “I just tried to step into the best version of myself, tap into all the presence and charm that I have — and it’s not as much as him — but, trying to take what was within me and just compounding on top of it.”.

It has been revealed that while “I Play Rocky” coincides with the 50th anniversary of the original “Rocky,” the movie also comes after Creed’s legacy has been pushed to the forefront of the franchise thanks to Michael B. Jordan and Ryan Coogler’s blockbuster “Creed” trilogy. During the press run, James joked about calling up his “son” Jordan (as the Oscar winner’s Adonis Creed is the love child of the late boxing champ) to talk about the family business.

Recent findings suggest that “I’ll tell you the truth: I did not call Mike, and we did not have this discussion,” James says, laughing. “But, I will say that I’m happy to be in the family.”.

In a recent development, to prepare for the role, James dropped between 20 and 25 pounds in two months and learned how to box for real. Read on for more about how he prepared for the part and the question he wishes he could’ve asked Weathers before production.

The list is far too long for the 10 minutes that we have right now.

Sources indicate that oh OK, cool. If I’m being honest, yeah, there are little white lies that you tell to help set yourself up for success. You don’t want to get caught in those lies too, though. So you want to make sure you can sort of deliver on it. Or that by the time they catch you in the lie, they love you so much that it doesn’t matter.

Yep, I’ll say I ride a horse. I own a horse. I’ve even put that on my resume. So, you know, whatever you got to do.

See, you believe me. That was good, right?

More than anything, it was just fun. So many times when you’re performing, I’ll have moments where I’m like, ‘Oh, I can’t even be around anyone,’ or I’m so locked in and so hyper focused on lines, or trying to stay in a in a vibe or a mood. That wasn’t this [movie] for me. This was Peter Farrelly giving me the keys to the scene and being like, ‘Go do your thing.’ So, it was very rewarding to see how it finally turned out.

There’s an internal litmus test that a lot of actors have. Maybe they’ll admit it. Maybe they won’t. But a part of it is when you read something and you’re like, “I don’t want to see anyone else do this.” Like, “I feel like I have the most to add to it or bring to it, and I don’t want to see anybody else’s version of this. I want to do my version.” So, that was a big deciding factor. Just reading it and being like, “No, it’s too special” on the page; I want to be able to do it myself. These characters that mean so much, that are so impactful, it’s an honor. It’s like why wouldn’t I want to have that you know on my belt if you will, that I got to play Carl Weathers. It’s amazing!

Sources indicate that his warmth was something that people don’t really get to see too much. Just looking at him, he could come across as like this physically imposing, maybe scary individual, but I’ve spoken to people who’ve spent a lot of real time with him, and you know they’ve all mentioned just how kind he was.

I tried to add that into the film just in terms of his relationship with Sly. When he finally admits that he’s not a boxer, and the fact that they could both laugh at that moment and then bond on something like, “Yes, we’re adversaries in this film, but, for the purposes of making this film, we’re gonna have to lock in and be able to trust each other, and it’d be nice if we liked each other too.”.

Recent findings suggest that I’d be keen to know if he really understood what he would mean to the legacy of this franchise, not only in the four “Rocky” films he made, but, if you count the “Creed” films [too]. The fact that there was a whole other world that spawned off people’s love for you and your character and your lineage, that we can make a whole series of movies about his son now.

It has been revealed that that really is Carl Weathers and his legacy. Not every actor rather is going to step into that role and last for four movies and then [influence] three more after that. Like, that’s because of him. So, I would wonder if he knew on those first days on “Rocky I,” like, did you ever think it could be this?

I was just over 200 pounds when I found out that I got this job and I found out that I had two months to get ready for this. So, my initial thought process was, “Let me just start eating and bulking up,” like protein for breakfast, lunch and dinner, just go ham. And I spoke to a trainer friend of mine, and he stated, if you work on cutting your body fat percentage down, effectively losing weight while keeping your muscle, you’ll be great. And people are gonna think you look bigger than you actually are. Trust me.

Industry observers note that so, that became my process: weight training at the gym in the morning; going down to Kingsway Boxing Club in Toronto with my trainer Jennifer Huggins and we just took it day by day, step by step. It started with cardio, just getting my endurance level up, then it was footwork. I didn’t realize how significant footwork was in boxing. Just learning how to not move around like a baby deer. And then unlearning all of those things to be the unpolished version of Apollo Creed. There were layers and levels to it. By the time I was done, I ended up dropping like 20-25 pounds and in the film, I’m 170-175 max.

I’m still healing from some of the punches I took, but it was a lot of fun to work with Anthony and spend so much time with him. Just getting close with him, building like a bond and a level of trust with each other. That’s crucial, time for character development. For us to actually be going through the motions of the choreography in that last fight scene, getting into the psychology of what it meant to be a boxer and respecting that art form, the process was equally as notable as the filming itself.

Sources indicate that first of all, I wear like the greatest suits ever, so that’s really fly. They’re all like custom made, so hopefully the production will give them to me afterward, because like who else are they gonna fit? So that’s been really really cool.

And then, just playing this young, smart, quick-witted lawyer has been really fun. I just feel like I’m stepping outside of myself and again giving the world something that they haven’t really seen me in.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nike stated Tuesday ahead of its first investor day in nine years that it was reaffirming its 2027 financial guidance.

The retailer also laid out a financial framework and mentioned that by the end of fiscal 2031 it's targeting approximately $5 billion in incremental revenue growth from fiscal year 2027, operating margins of 12% to 14% and adjusted earnings per share of $3.00 to $3.50. The company said higher-quality revenue, gross margin expansion and productivity improvements would help it reach its goals.

Nike's 2027 financial guidance includes expectations for revenue to decline in the high-single-digit range, an adjusted operating margin of approximately 6%, and adjusted EPS of $1.15 to $1.35.

The company also introduced a strategy it's calling Full Stride Ahead, which the company said aims "to get closer to athletes and focus resources on the greatest opportunities for long-term growth.".

Nike CEO Elliott Hill told CNBC's Sara Eisen that the new initiative is about "being closer to the athletes we serve.".

"What's different today is the depth and breadth we're taking from an innovation perspective," Hill noted.

In a recent development, he added that Nike is emphasizing sportswear at a time when sports have never been more relevant around the world. Hill also noted Nike is working to regain its cultural relevance, after a perceived dropoff contributed to its slowdown both in its home market and in China.

Nike said it would focus on performance sports and sportswear opportunities "with the greatest potential for long-term growth," and said its five priority sports would be running, training, global football, basketball and outdoor.

Nike is holding an investor day at its Oregon headquarters Tuesday as the organization aims to prove to investors that its turnaround strategy is yielding success after a yearslong slump.

Last month, the manufacturer reported mixed fiscal first-quarter results as it revealed a restructuring plan, including layoffs that it said would start next year. It's the company's third round of layoffs to be announced this year.

Nike's net income and revenue both fell during the most recent period compared with a year ago, and the company said it expects revenue to decline by a high single-digit percentage in fiscal 2027.

According to recent reports, the latest strategy, dubbed Pace, focuses on the company's supply chain and reorganizing into three geographies. Nike said the turnaround strategy is expected to deliver roughly $2.5 billion in savings through fiscal 2031.

Nike has been seeing significant sustained declines in its China market, where revenue last quarter dropped 26%. Experts have said the tech giant is losing relevance in the country, while Nike has said it's actively working to win over younger consumers.

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, Nike revealed last quarter that it's creating a newly introduced global campus in India as part of its new growth strategy, hoping the country will help boost its performance. The company remarked it was remaining focused on China even as it begins to build out its India presence.

Nike COO Venkatesh Alagirisamy told CNBC the manufacturer sees an opportunity to triple its business in the country over the next five years.

He added that Nike's broader strategy will position it for success in India.

"If you look at the three components, brand building, landing those innovations into marketplaces in an increasingly locally connected fashion and then doing all of those things in a much faster pace really aligns well with the aspirations for India," he remarked.

CEO Elliott Hill's turnaround strategy includes improving different parts of the business at different rates based on priority. While it's seen some signs of progress in the North America business, Hill has noted that performance isn't enough to offset the pressures on the company elsewhere, including internationally.

The Nike consumer has also been under increased macroeconomic pressure as geopolitical tensions mount and inflation rises.

Shares of Nike have fallen 50% over the past two years.

Watchmaker Denis Flageollet founded De Bethune in 2002 with art collector David Zanetta. According to recent reports, watchmaker Felix Baumgartner and chief designer Martin Frei co-founded Urwerk in 1997, naming the brand for the Mesopotamian city of Ur, where Sumerians pioneered timekeeping. According to recent reports, named after watchmaker François Czapek, who founded his firm in 1845, the Geneva-based brand was revived in 2015 to honor his legacy. The latest model, the 40.5mm Antarctique Tourbillon Victory Green, got its start as a bespoke order and now is available in a limited series of 10 numbered pieces, each one produced on demand. At Cellini Jewelers, New York.

Master watch restorer Michel Parmigiani founded his firm in Fleurier, Switzerland, in 1996. This month, he won the Chronograph Prize at the 2026 Grand Prix d’Horlogerie de Genève, the Oscars of watchmaking, for the Tonda PF Chronographe Mystérieux — its styling is similar to this Toric Petite Seconde Platinum Morning Blue, which debuted in October. At Feldmar Watch Organization, Los Angeles.

Geneva’s MB&F debuted in 2005 as a concept house, in which founder Maximilian Büsser would partner with independent watchmakers and artisans. Limited to 33 pieces, the LM1 EVO offers two separate time displays and an oversized flying balance wheel suspended above the movement. At MB&F Lab at Westime, Beverly Hills.

Industrial designer Benoît Mintiens founded Ressence in 2010 in Antwerp, Belgium, crafting pieces that tell time using a system of orbiting, rotating discs. Weighing just 82 grams, the Type 10 DN is seamlessly crafted of two independent sections, allowing the movement to function while the display above is filled with oil. At Feldmar Watch Organization, Los Angeles.

Sources indicate that heinrich Moser founded his namesake brand in 1828; 174 years later, his great-grandson relaunched it in northern Switzerland. This Heritage Centre Seconds Espresso Fumé honors the early 20th century moment when wristwatches became the preferred timekeeping device over pocket watches. At Westime, Rodeo Drive.

Latest Update: A mysterious twist in the universe’s oldest light could reveal latest physics

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1623 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A mysterious twist in the universe's oldest light could offer clues to physics that scientists have yet to discover.
  • The mystery centers on the cosmic microwave background (CMB), a faint glow of radiation left over from approximately 380,000 years after the Significant Bang.
  • Industry observers note that when the universe was about 380,000 years old, it had cooled enough to become transparent, allowing light to travel freely through space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A mysterious twist in the universe's oldest light could offer clues to physics that scientists have yet to discover. But before researchers can determine whether this subtle signal reveals something extraordinary about the cosmos, they must answer a crucial question: Is the effect actually coming from the universe, or could it be an illusion created by the telescopes observing it?

The mystery centers on the cosmic microwave background (CMB), a faint glow of radiation left over from approximately 380,000 years after the Significant Bang. This ancient light provides a remarkable snapshot of the "baby universe" as it existed nearly 13.8 billion years ago, allowing scientists to investigate conditions from the earliest stages of cosmic history.

Industry observers note that when the universe was about 380,000 years old, it had cooled enough to become transparent, allowing light to travel freely through space. As radiation scattered off free electrons during this transition, it acquired a small amount of linear polarization. Polarization describes the direction in which light's electric field oscillates, and a similar effect occurs when sunlight scatters through Earth's atmosphere.

Industry observers note that now, observations suggest that the polarization of this ancient radiation may have shifted slightly as the light traveled across the universe. This possible rotation, called cosmic birefringence, is especially intriguing because it could point to physical processes not explained by the Standard Model, the leading theory describing fundamental particles and their interactions. Confirming the effect might even provide fresh insights into dark matter and dark energy (see Sidebar).

A Mysterious Cosmic Signal or a Telescope Error?

Recent findings suggest that there is a major obstacle to interpreting this potential discovery. An extremely small error in how a telescope's polarization detectors are aligned can produce a signal that looks almost identical to cosmic birefringence.

To help address this problem, physicists at the University of California San Diego developed a newly introduced technique for checking how accurately different groups of detectors measure polarization angles. They tested their approach using existing observations collected by the European Space Agency's Planck satellite, which mapped the universe's ancient radiation in extraordinary detail.

The research was led by Postdoctoral Fellow Anto I. Lonappan, Chancellor's Distinguished Professor of Physics Brian Keating, and Associate Professor of Physics Kam Arnold. Their findings were published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Separating Real Cosmic Effects From Instrument Errors.

Recent findings suggest that previous studies have suggested that the polarization of the CMB may have rotated by just a fraction of a degree over its nearly 14 billion years of travel. Although that sounds insignificant, such a tiny change could have enormous implications for fundamental physics.

Industry observers note that unfortunately, a telescope whose polarization detectors are misaligned by a similarly small angle could produce precisely the same apparent rotation. If every detector shares the same alignment error, the resulting measurements cannot distinguish that error from a genuine rotation of the cosmic signal.

Sources indicate that the UC San Diego researchers found a way to investigate the problem from another angle. Rather than relying on a single combined measurement, they compared separate polarization maps generated by different groups of detectors.

Sources indicate that if cosmic birefringence is real, its effect should appear consistently across all these maps. By comparing the maps with one another, the researchers can effectively eliminate any rotation shared by all of them. What remains reveals differences in the calibration of the individual detector groups, making it possible to identify inconsistencies that might otherwise complicate the search for new physics.

"The signal we are looking for is incredibly small, so we have to be certain that we are seeing the universe and not our instrument," mentioned Lonappan. "Our method gives us a complementary way to check that distinction. Before interpreting a tiny rotation as new physics, we want to know that the calibration itself can be trusted.".

Testing the Mystery With Planck Satellite Data.

It has been revealed that to evaluate their technique, the researchers analyzed eight polarization maps produced using Planck observations. They then compared their findings with results from an established approach called the Minami-Komatsu analysis, which is used to distinguish instrumental rotation from possible cosmic birefringence.

It has been revealed that although the two methods rely on different assumptions, they produced consistent results. This agreement provides an important independent check on how relative detector calibration errors are being assessed.

In a recent development, the upcoming approach also has a deliberate limitation. Because it removes any rotation common to all the maps, it cannot independently measure the overall polarization angle or determine how much the universe itself may have rotated the light. Establishing that absolute rotation still requires an independent reference for calibrating the overall angle.

To demonstrate how their findings fit with existing measurements, the researchers combined their reconstruction of relative calibration differences with the common calibration value inferred from the established analysis. This produced an estimated cosmic birefringence angle of 0.37 ± 0.12 degrees, matching the Minami-Komatsu result.

Importantly, this agreement does not independently confirm that the ancient light has actually rotated. Instead, it shows that the new method can reproduce results from the existing framework while providing a separate way to examine potential calibration problems.

Searching for Gravitational Waves From the Early Universe.

The technique could also play an important role in another major pursuit in cosmology: the search for gravitational waves generated during the universe's earliest moments.

To understand why, scientists distinguish between two patterns of polarization in the cosmic microwave background, known as E modes and B modes.

It has been revealed that E modes were first detected in 2002. They arise from density variations in the early universe and form symmetric polarization patterns. B modes have a different appearance, featuring patterns that resemble curls or swirls.

One known source of B modes is gravitational lensing, which occurs when the gravity of matter between Earth and the early universe bends and distorts the path of ancient light. Scientists have already observed B modes created through this process.

Industry observers note that however, researchers are also searching for a different kind of B mode that could have been produced by primordial gravitational waves. These ripples in spacetime may have originated during an extremely early period of rapid cosmic expansion, known as inflation. The distinctive B mode signal associated with those primordial gravitational waves has not yet been detected.

Finding it would provide powerful evidence about gravitational waves in the early universe and could offer strong support for particular models of cosmic inflation, potentially transforming scientists' understanding of how the universe began.

Why Extremely Precise Measurements Matter.

Sources indicate that the challenge is that even a slight error in a telescope's polarization calibration can cause some of the much stronger E-mode signal to appear incorrectly as B modes. This contamination could make an instrumental artifact look like an exciting cosmological discovery.

The UC San Diego method could help prevent such mistakes by identifying differences in polarization angle calibration among detector groups. That makes it a potentially valuable tool for future experiments searching for the extremely faint signatures of primordial gravitational waves.

In a recent development, this kind of independent verification will become increasingly crucial as observatories develop the ability to measure cosmic polarization with greater precision. One example is the Simons Observatory, where Keating serves as principal investigator.

As these instruments become more sensitive, researchers will need equally rigorous methods for confirming that the faint signals they detect are genuine features of the universe rather than imperfections in their equipment.

"The detection of primordial B modes would transform our understanding of the early universe, so the measurement must survive rigorous calibration checks," said Keating. "Anto has developed a useful fresh framework for testing relative polarization-angle calibration. This is ultimately about knowing when we can trust a measurement.".

Beyond the Standard Model: Dark Matter and Dark Energy.

The possibility of cosmic birefringence is particularly fascinating because it could reveal physics that lies beyond the Standard Model.

Recent findings suggest that although this framework has been remarkably successful at describing fundamental particles and their interactions, it cannot explain everything in the universe. Among its most notable unanswered questions are the identity of dark matter and the origin and observed magnitude of dark energy. Together, these mysterious components account for approximately 95% of the universe's total energy density.

It has been revealed that one possible explanation for cosmic birefringence involves a hypothetical field associated with particles resembling axions. Such a field could interact with light and gradually alter its polarization as it crosses the universe. However, these particles have not been confirmed to exist, and they would not necessarily be responsible for dark matter.

Other theoretical explanations connect the possible rotation to fields associated with dark energy, the mysterious phenomenon linked to the accelerating expansion of the universe.

If cosmic birefringence is eventually confirmed, it could provide an entirely new way to investigate these cosmic mysteries and reveal evidence of physical laws beyond those at the moment understood.

It has been revealed that for now, the first challenge is ensuring that the subtle signal can be trusted. By giving researchers another way to identify potential measurement errors, the new technique strengthens the foundation for future discoveries that could reshape our picture of the universe.

Materials provided by University of California - San Diego. Original written by Michelle Franklin. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

How the ‘Elsinore’ Makeup Team Transformed Stars Andrew Scott and Olivia Colman to Bring the Story of Ian Charleson to Life

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In “Elsinore,” Andrew Scott plays real-life actor Ian Charleson, who performed his final role while dying of AIDS.
  • Written by Stephen Beresford, “Elsinore” follows the deeply emotional and inspirational true story of Charleson as he confronts his mortality with courage, honesty and wit.
  • The biopic (currently in theaters) reunites Scott with Olivia Colman, who previously starred alongside him in “Fleabag.” This time, their bond is a special one as Colman plays Margaret Johnson, the doctor who treats Charleson.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In “Elsinore,” Andrew Scott plays real-life actor Ian Charleson, who performed his final role while dying of AIDS.

Written by Stephen Beresford, “Elsinore” follows the deeply emotional and inspirational true story of Charleson as he confronts his mortality with courage, honesty and wit. On Nov. 13, 1989, Charleson walked onto the stage at London’s National Theatre to play Hamlet for the last time. He was dying of AIDS, a fact he kept secret. Very few of the 1,000 audience members at the Olivier Theatre knew his story. Related Stories Qatar Film Chief Hassan Al Thawadi States World Cup Success Paved Way for Hollywood Push, Signals Next Steps on Neon Deal Judge Allows Trump to Sue Fresh York Times Reporters Over Tax Fraud Claims.

The biopic (currently in theaters) reunites Scott with Olivia Colman, who previously starred alongside him in “Fleabag.” This time, their bond is a special one as Colman plays Margaret Johnson, the doctor who treats Charleson.

Recent findings suggest that for “Elsinore,” both actors needed to transform themselves — not only into the real people they were portraying, but also back to the 1980s. That’s where makeup department head Nadia Stacey played a key role. Stacey, who was honored at last month’s Middleburg Film Festival, spoke about her work and approach to the film, explaining that “when there are real people, you have to be sympathetic to them.”.

It has been revealed that stacey described the ’80s as a tricky period to recreate, given it can easily become clichéd. “You immediately imagine everybody had a perm,” she remarked. “My approach every time is that you shouldn’t notice hair and makeup unless you actually want to notice hair and makeup. The story told itself. I just needed to tell his journey and put us in the era we were in without overdoing it.”.

It has been revealed that stacey worked to achieve a look that embodied Scott’s portrayal of Charleson while keeping everything authentic. “We know Andrew as that — jet black hair and brown eyes,” Stacey explained. Charleson, however, had blonde hair and blue eyes. “We didn’t want to push something too far to jar the audience. Andrew and I talked about it, and we said we should approach it in the sense of how an actor at that time would have done it. They would have been dyeing their hair themselves.” Instead of bleaching Scott’s hair, Stacey gave him a full head of blonde highlights and blue contact lenses, capturing Charleson’s defining characteristics.

Industry observers note that she would also track his journey after Charleson tested positive for HIV in 1986. As Charleson’s health declined, Stacey discolored Scott’s skin tone and added dark circles. For the sarcoma lesions, she used tattoo transfers, which she applied to Scott’s body.

Joining Stacey for the conversation was Colman, who also underwent a transformation to play Johnson. “The second you put a wig on someone, as an audience, you know they’re wearing a wig. So it’s hard to make sure that it looks good,” Stacey remarked. “I felt like we were telling a story about real people, and we needed to be as close to that as possible without pulling her out of the story. But from all the photos we had of Margaret, we know she had this blonde bob, so we tried it.” And it worked.

Colman had also done her research on playing Johnson and knew how key it was to stay as close to the character as possible. She recalled, “We tried on the wig in the makeup room, and because I had been watching Margaret, I was very much up for a wig.”.

Colman pointed out that the film doesn’t glorify Charleson’s death. Throughout the film, casting director Jessica Ronane cast background actors who actually knew him. David Rintoul — Charleson’s actual best friend — plays the Ghost of Hamlet’s father. Some of the hospital cast were also friends of the late actor.

Colman shared, “The most interesting thing about finding out about Ian is every single person he spoke to said, ‘Ian was hilarious. Ian was funny.’ And so they wanted that. Everybody that they approached said, ‘Absolutely. Yes, please, count me in.’”.

Sources indicate that in the film’s final act, Johnson comes to see Charleson. The camera focuses primarily on Johnson being moved by his performance. “Andrew, bless his heart, came to be there that day. It was only on me, and they’d already filmed the other bits, but he insisted. On a very long, exhausting shoot, on his day off, he came in and remarked, ‘Absolutely, I’ll do it for you.’ So he was performing bits of ‘Hamlet’ for me.”.

Fast forward to the film’s premiere at the London Film Festival, and Colman reflected, “I cried as it started till the end and had to pass tissues to the person next to me as well. And I think, for me, even though I’d seen it, it was seeing him in it and what it took to do that. He’s so incredible and so generous and so fun. Honestly, if I could just choose a handful of people to work for the rest of my career, he would absolutely be one of them.”.

Colman also shared the film’s powerful response: “There’s something beautiful about film reminding you of these past heroes.”.
