Which MacBook to Buy (2026): Here’s Which Laptop Is Right for You

📅 08 Feb 2018 | ⏱️ 31 min read (6161 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~31 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • MacBooks went to some adventurous latest places this year.
  • Having tested every fresh MacBook you can buy, I can guide you to the right laptop for your budget and performance needs.
  • For more recommendations, check out the rest of our computer buying guides, like Best Laptops, Best Mac Desktops, Best Cheap Laptops, Best iPads, and Best MacBook Accessories.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MacBooks went to some adventurous latest places this year. The MacBook Neo pushes the boundaries of how cheap and low-powered a MacBook could go, while the OLED MacBook Pro takes it in the opposite direction. While the midyear price hike put a damper on all the new releases, prices won’t be going down anytime soon.

Having tested every fresh MacBook you can buy, I can guide you to the right laptop for your budget and performance needs.

For more recommendations, check out the rest of our computer buying guides, like Best Laptops, Best Mac Desktops, Best Cheap Laptops, Best iPads, and Best MacBook Accessories.

Updated November 2026: I’ve added notes from my testing of the M6 MacBook Pro and OLED MacBook Pros, along with additional buying advice given the new prices and rumors about future updates.

Although the MacBook Neo is more affordable, and the M5 MacBook Pro offers a better display with the far more powerful M5 Pro and Max chips, the MacBook Air remains the model I recommend for most people. The 2026 M5 refresh isn’t particularly exciting, but if your livelihood depends on sitting in front of a MacBook all day, it’s the best option.

The starting price for the 13-inch model is now $1,299, up $200 from before. Notably, for much of last year, you could buy this laptop for as little as $750. That’s a painful reality, but it doesn’t change my recommendation that this is the MacBook model most people should buy.

Industry observers note that although the exterior of the MacBook Air hasn’t changed since 2021, Apple has slowly evolved the laptop into something that feels airy and near-weightless. Most customers need not worry about having too many tabs or applications open, eating up all that memory. You won’t be sitting around waiting for a file to download, because the SSD is blazing fast. With support for up to two 5K external monitors, the MacBook Air can function as a proper workstation when paired with a docking station. The 12-megapixel, 1080p webcam is plenty good for video calls.

What matters most is that the M5 can do far more than most people will ever ask of their MacBook Air. Apple has boosted the GPU so much over the past generations that the M5 is actually on par with the M3 Pro. You’ll probably spend most of your day in browser tabs, Slack, Zoom, office applications, and spreadsheets, but the MacBook Air can just as easily handle Photoshop or Lightroom. You can even dabble in video editing or some light gaming if you want. If you were a professional video editor, you’d likely be bothered by the render times. But if it’s more of a hobby or side project, the M5 MacBook Air likely won’t impede your flow. Again, that’s where the MacBook Air really lives up to its do-it-all reputation.

As always, there are two sizes, measured diagonally: 13.6-inch and 15.3-inch. Aside from the $200 price gap, the screen size and speakers are the only notable differences between the two. Apple even scales up the pixel density to make sure the display on the 15-inch model looks just as sharp. The speakers on the 15-inch model sound incredible, second only to the 16-inch MacBook Pro. But choosing between the two sizes really comes down to how you use your laptop. If you have it plugged into an external monitor most days, you may as well get the 13-inch model and save yourself the extra space when you need to carry it around. But if a laptop is your primary machine, having that 15.3-inch screen really makes a difference, especially for more complicated applications or for using Split View.

As you may notice, the M5 MacBook Air now starts with 512 GB of storage. That’s twice what previous models packed and helps to rationalize the price gap between the Neo and the Air. Having 512 GB of storage means you won’t have to worry about filling up your drive right away. This kind of headroom allows the technology to fade into the background—a design philosophy Apple has always championed. If you are a power user, consider adding more memory. Remember, MacBook memory and internal storage aren’t expandable down the road.

Read my in-depth comparison of the MacBook Neo and MacBook Air to see how they stack up.

Recent findings suggest that after years of rumors, Apple has launched a upcoming MacBook Pro with never-before-seen features—most notably, the tandem PROLED XDR touchscreen. That’s right: this MacBook Pro is the first to ever have a touch-capable display, and you can now interact with it directly with your finger. Many people will be drawn in by the novelty of the feature (even though it’s been available on Windows laptops for almost a decade now), but I am skeptical about how useful it will be for day-to-day tasks. You will still primarily use the keyboard and trackpad, but I can see how the touchscreen would help in certain situations. Apple has made some optimizations to make the interface more touch-friendly, though I think there’s still room for improvement.

But don’t get me wrong: This MacBook Pro’s screen is the real deal. I’ve never seen a screen quite like this. Despite OLED’s reputation for not being bright enough, Apple’s is different. It delivers the insane contrast and clarity you’d expect from OLED, but with a maximum brightness that’s hundreds of nits higher than the previous-gen Mini-LED MacBook Pros.

Industry observers note that it has a few tricks up its sleeve too, such as the return of the glow-up Apple logo on the lid and the hole-punch camera to replace the notch. As someone who has never gotten used to that ugly notch, that might be the change I was most thrilled to see. Apple even brought Dynamic Island from the iPhone to the MacBook Pro, using that hole creatively while hiding the camera. All in all, there’s a lot to be impressed by here.

Industry observers note that the only real concern is that it still uses the older M5 Pro or M5 Max chip. These are still some of Apple’s most powerful chips, but they have been out for over a year. This is the first time Apple isn’t introducing upcoming chips alongside its new MacBook Pro in the past six years. Rumors indicate that the organization may be skipping the M6 Pro and M6 Max altogether. That’s made stranger by the fact that Apple is keeping the previous-gen models in the lineup—another uncommon move.

According to recent reports, there’s a $400 difference between the 2025 M5 Pro and the 2025 PROLED M5 Pro, and for this pro-level demographic of buyers, it’s a relatively small price to pay for all the upgrades. I appreciate that Apple kept the older models around for those who want the extra performance without the fancy, more expensive display. On the other hand, if Apple wasn’t right now selling them, third-party retailers might have dropped the price more while they were still in stock.

It has been revealed that the MacBook Neo (7/10, WIRED Recommends) came out earlier this year, and it had a lot to prove. That’s especially true since it debuted at just $599, an unheard-of price point for Apple laptops—much less than any other model, even before recent price hikes took effect. And even though the MacBook Neo now starts at $699 after those price increases, it remains an aggressively affordable option. To keep pricing low, Apple had to make the following compromises:.

According to recent reports, that’s a major list, and the memory limitation is the most significant drawback. Unlike on the MacBook Air, you can find the limits of the Neo fairly easily—and not on purpose. If you’re coming from a 16 GB MacBook Air, for example, you likely developed a habit of keeping idle applications or tabs open. On the MacBook Neo, you’ll need to be a bit more aware of what’s open to avoid slowdowns. You’ll also want to know which ports you’re using, since only the rear USB-C port supports an external display. The other USB-C port is only USB 2.0, rated at a max of 480 megabits per second. That’s definitely not the one you want to use for file transfers. If you don’t have the Touch ID model, you may even need to watch who you’re sitting next to in a coffee shop when entering passwords. We haven’t had to worry about these things on laptops for many years.

According to recent reports, in exchange, Apple delivers an incredible front-of-screen experience on the MacBook Neo, never before seen on a laptop of this price. The display is sharper and brighter than anything else you can buy for $699, while the keyboard and trackpad are both excellent. Build quality is every bit as strong as any other Apple product, and at 0.50 inches thick, it’s still quite portable.

On top of all that, the Neo has three really good features over the Air. There’s a wider range of color options—and a lot of people will gravitate toward the Neo for that alone. My favorite change is the lack of a camera notch. While the bezels are slightly thicker, I’d still prefer a uniform screen without an ugly notch blocking part of my view. Perhaps most meaningfully, the Neo is reportedly the most repairable MacBook in the lineup, swapping out adhesives for screws on components such as the battery and speakers. This is great for classrooms and businesses hoping to keep fleets of these up to date without contributing as much to the mounting e-waste problem.

Industry observers note that for most of the time, you’ll enjoy using the MacBook Neo. As a parent, this should be the go-to device for high school and college students. It also works equally well as a secondary laptop away from your workstation or as a small travel laptop.

The newer PROLED MacBook Pros are flashier, but they use the same M5 Pro or M5 Max chips as the previous-gen models. And interestingly, Apple still sells these older ones. So, while these 2025 models don’t have touchscreen OLED displays, they’re every bit as powerful. You aren’t missing out on any performance, and if the rumors hold, these will be the top-of-the-line MacBook Pro chips for a while.

Of course, these MacBook Pros are still very expensive, though. Like its PROLED sibling, the standard M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro (8/10, WIRED Recommends) aren’t for the average person. The price alone should clue you in, but if you are the target audience and willing to pay well over $4,000 for a powerful laptop, the M5 Max MacBook Pro is unmatched in its capabilities. As always, the “Max” is primarily about considerably more GPU performance. Along with the option of two extra CPU cores, you can get up to 40 GPU cores, each with a built-in AI accelerator.

Recent findings suggest that the M5 Max’s power applies to three use cases: creative applications, on-device AI processing, and gaming. Whether it’s 3D modeling, video editing, or some other resource-heavy application, the M5 Max MacBook Pro will tear through it. But AI performance also takes a significant leap. I tested a 17-billion-parameter Llama-2 model, which ran at conversational speed locally (the speed an AI model runs on a device), and it was 31 percent faster than running the same model on the M3 Max MacBook Pro.

Sources indicate that then there’s gaming. Nobody is going to buy the MacBook Pro for its gaming prowess alone, but it’s there when you want it. For the first time ever, you can hit over 60 frames per second in Cyberpunk 2077 on the Ultra preset with no upscaling. That’s an RTX 5070 Ti-level of laptop gaming performance. And unlike laptops that actually have that GPU, the MacBook Pro gets incredible battery life. Lastly, creative professionals will appreciate the faster storage speeds than previous generations.

The Mini-LED display is as gorgeous as ever, even if it pales in comparison to the new OLED models. You get a solid selection of ports, including three Thunderbolt 5 ports that offer ample external display support. It’s at the top of its class in nearly every aspect. Beyond CPU/GPU performance, you can choose between two screen sizes that perform similarly.

Recent findings suggest that if this machine is overkill, you can drop down to the M5 Pro, which starts at $2,499 but is a power champ in its own right. Its multi-core and GPU performance are also stronger than the fresh M6 (see below).

The MacBook Pro is a slight misnomer because there are really three variants. I’ve talked about the PROLED and M5 Pro/M5 Max versions above. The third, the base model, is the upcoming M6 MacBook Pro, and despite using the latest chip, it’s the cheapest of the Pro options. Unfortunately, it’s also the hardest to recommend. That has less to do with the laptop itself and more to do with its price and how it fits into the lineup.

Sources indicate that like its M5 predecessor, it remains a beautiful, well-made laptop with all the high-end features you’d expect from a MacBook Pro. That includes the excellent speakers and very bright Mini-LED display. But it costs $1,999. Keep in mind that the M5 Pro MacBook Pro is $2,499, and you can still buy the M5 model for $1,799 or the 15-inch M5 MacBook Air for $1,499—hence the “awkward middle child” designation.

To be fair, you get a terabyte of storage and 16 GB of RAM, while the M5 MacBook Pro started with 512 GB of storage. Apple also kept the starting price the same—that is, the price after Apple increased pricing across the board (the base MacBook Pro used to start at $1,699), but let’s not go there.

The M6 chip is certainly faster than the M5, but it’s less of a major leap forward than in previous generations. You’re looking at about a 15 percent improvement in CPU performance. I think the bigger disappointment is only a 9 percent improvement in graphics. That’s been an area where previous generational chip leaps have been more significant.

If you are considering the M6 MacBook Pro, I strongly suggest you look at the 15-inch M5 MacBook Air. It starts at a much lower price for the base configuration, but you can bump up the specs and still stay below $2,000. Yes, the MacBook Air is a different machine, but it has the performance that would impress many MacBook Pro customers.

Sources indicate that all MacBooks were updated in 2026, making it a good time to buy one. The problem is that on June 25, Apple dramatically increased the price of all the MacBooks (and iPads) to varying degrees. Here’s a breakdown of the new starting prices, with increases ranging from $100 to $400:.

Recent findings suggest that it’s rare for Apple to raise prices suddenly, especially when the change doesn’t coincide with a product refresh. What made this revision especially unusual, though, is that only a few months had passed since the MacBook Neo rolled out. Apple blamed the price spikes on memory and storage increases, stating that AI data centers had “created an extraordinary surge in demand” never seen before.

So yes, the better time to buy a MacBook would have been earlier this year. While Apple notes that it is “working tirelessly to find solutions,” I wouldn’t expect these prices to come down anytime soon. Predictions around how long this memory shortage will last are measured in years, not months.

Industry observers note that currently, only the 14-inch MacBook Pro gets the latest M6 chip. Rumors suggest Apple will skip the M6 Pro and M6 Max in this generation, saving the chip update for the MacBook Pro until the M7 Pro and M7 Max.

A Breakdown of Each M-Series Chip.

Apple’s processors are scattered across different MacBook models, and you can find older models online from third-party retailers, either upcoming or refurbished. If you do stumble upon older chips, you might be wondering how they compare to newer options. Here, get a breakdown of the differences to consider.

According to recent reports, M6: Apple has already released its latest M6 line of chips, though the rollout has been slower than normal. As of this year, it’s only available in the base 14-inch MacBook Pro, iMac, and Mac Mini. I expect to see this arrive on devices like the iPad Pro and MacBook Air eventually, but the rumors about the rest of the M6 lineup are perplexing. Reports indicate Apple will skip the M6 Pro and M6 Max entirely and jump straight to the M7 Pro and M7 Max, perhaps in late 2027. That makes sense given what Apple just launched with the OLED MacBook Pro, which uses the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as the previous generation.

According to recent reports, M5: Apple launched the M5 chips in late 2025 with the 14-inch MacBook Pro, iPad Pro, and Vision Pro. The base M5 offers up to a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU, though a lower-tier 9-core CPU is still available on the iPad Pro. The M5 is about 10 to 15 percent faster in CPU performance than the M4 and takes a significant step up in GPU, AI workloads, and even storage speed. The M5 is now also available on the MacBook Air.

Sources indicate that M5 Pro: These more powerful M5 chips are at the moment available in the 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pros. The M5 Pro comes with a 15-core CPU and a 16-core GPU, with an option to upgrade to an 18-core CPU and a 20-core GPU. As with previous generations, the Pro chip gets all the same benefits as those in the M5 architecture but adds more cores and improved memory bandwidth. The biggest advantage is in GPU and on-device AI performance. This time around, however, both the M5 Pro and M5 Max also debuted the “Fusion Architecture,” a latest version of UltraFusion (previously used only on the Ultra chips) that combines two dies across a superfast interconnect.

In a recent development, M5 Max: The M5 Max is the M5 Pro—only with more GPU power. You can get up to 40 GPU cores, putting the MacBook Pro on par with high-end gaming laptops in graphics performance. With neural accelerators built into each GPU core, you’ve got one of the most powerful AI laptops on the market. It comes in either the MacBook Pro or the Mac Studio.

According to recent reports, M5 Ultra: Like the other “Ultra” chips, the M5 Ultra is available only in the 2026 Mac Studio. It’s by far Apple’s most powerful chip, but you can’t configure it in a MacBook.

M4: The M4 launched in 2024. It has a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU. Apple claims the M4 delivers 1.8 times faster CPU performance and 2.2 times faster GPU performance than the M1. Meanwhile, the neural engine is more than three times faster than the original and twice as fast as the M3. It also starts with 16 GB of unified memory, which helps to power Apple Intelligence (the tech giant’s suite of artificial intelligence features) more smoothly. It’s available on the 14-inch MacBook Pro (2024), iMac (2024), and MacBook Air (13-inch and 15-inch, 2025).

According to recent reports, M4 Pro: The M4 Pro has a 14-core CPU (which Apple claims is up to 1.9 times faster than the M1 Pro) and up to a 20-core GPU, with up to 64 GB of unified memory. Built on a second-generation 3-nanometer process, it also supports enhanced GPU features like mesh shading and ray tracing—the latter of which is now twice as fast as on M3 chips. You’ll find it on the 2024 MacBook Pro (14-inch and 16-inch) and Mac Mini (2024).

M4 Max: This chip has a 16-core CPU and up to a 40-core GPU with support for up to 128 GB of unified memory. Apple says the CPU is up to 2.2 times faster than the M1 Max, while the GPU is up to 1.9 times faster. Like the M4 Pro, it supports mesh shading and ray tracing. The M4 Max is available as an option on the 2024 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro, and you can also get it as an option in the current Mac Studio.

M3: The M3 was available on the 14-inch MacBook Pro (late 2023), 13-inch MacBook Air (2024), 15-inch MacBook Air (2024), and 24-inch iMac (2023). It packs an 8-core CPU and up to a 10-core GPU, with up to 24 GB of unified memory. Compared with the M1, Apple claimed CPU performance was up to 35 percent faster and GPU performance up to 65 percent faster. The company remarked the CPU and GPU are both 20 percent faster than the M2. As with the M1 and M2, it was great for basic tasks like word processing, sending emails, using spreadsheets, and light gaming. The 13-inch and 15-inch MacBook Air also supported two external displays (one up to 6K at 60 Hz and another up to 5K at 60 Hz).

It has been revealed that M3 Pro: With a 12-core CPU and an 18-core GPU, Apple claimed the M3 Pro’s GPU was only up to 10 percent faster than the M2 Pro, making it a marginal upgrade from its predecessor. Compared with the M1 Pro, however, the M2 Pro was up to 40 percent faster in GPU performance and 20 percent faster in CPU performance. It was available on the 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro from 2023. It was the ideal in-between for those who needed a chip more powerful than the M3 but didn’t need the full power of the M3 Max.

M3 Max: The next step up from the M2 Max. It had a 16-core CPU, 40-core GPU, and up to 128 GB of unified memory. According to Apple, the CPU performance was up to 80 percent faster than the M1 Max and up to 50 percent faster than the M2 Max. As for GPU performance, it was said to be up to 50 percent faster than the M1 Max and 20 percent faster than the M2 Max. The M3 Max was available on the 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro (late 2023).

Sources indicate that M3 Ultra: Apple introduced the M3 lineup in 2023, but only announced the M3 Ultra in 2025. It was even better than the latest M4 Max and M5 at the time. It had up to 32 CPU cores (24 performance cores) and up to 80 GPU cores. Apple claimed it was up to 2.5 times faster than the M1 Ultra. It also came with 96 GB of unified memory, upgradable to 512 GB, and up to 16 TB of SSD storage. This chip was available only on the 2025 Mac Studio.

It has been revealed that M2: The M2 was an entry-level chip like the M1, with slightly more processing power. It packed an 8-core CPU and up to a 10-core GPU (two more GPU cores than its predecessor), and supported up to 24 GB of unified memory. Apple mentioned the second-generation chip has an 18 percent faster CPU and a GPU that’s 35 percent more powerful than its earlier version. The M2 was great for daily tasks like word processing and web browsing, but tasks such as editing multiple streams of 4K footage and 3D rendering should be reserved for Pro or Max chips. It was available in the MacBook Air (13-inch, 2022), MacBook Air (15-inch, 2022), and MacBook Pro (13-inch, 2022).

M2 Pro: The M2 Pro had up to 12 cores in the CPU and up to a 19-core GPU, with up to 32 GB of unified memory. Apple claimed performance was up to 20 percent faster than with the 10-core M1 Pro and graphics were 30 percent faster. We recommended this chip for intermediate video and photo editors. It was a marginal upgrade compared with the M1 Pro, but it was the best option for those who wanted a more future-proof processor. You could find it in the MacBook Pro (14-inch and 16-inch) from early 2023 and the Mac Mini (2023).

Recent findings suggest that M2 Max: The M2 Max packs up to a 12-core CPU and up to a 38-core GPU (with support for up to 96 GB of unified memory). According to Apple, graphics are 30 percent faster than on the M1 Max. The M2 Max is an excellent choice for those who work with graphics-intensive content, including graphic design, 3D modeling, and heavy-duty video footage. But as with the M2 Pro, it’s an incremental upgrade if you’re coming from an M1 Max. It’s available in the MacBook Pro (14-inch and 16-inch) released in early 2023 and the Mac Studio (2023).

It has been revealed that M2 Ultra: The successor to the M1 Ultra, the M2 Ultra was available in the second-generation Mac Studio and the Mac Pro (2023). Composed of two M2 Max chips, using Apple’s UltraFusion technology, the M2 Ultra had a 24-core CPU and a GPU configurable with 60 or 76 cores. Apple claimed the CPU delivered up to 20 percent faster performance and that the GPU was up to 30 percent faster than the M1 Ultra. This was the chip to get if you were working with extremely heavy-duty content that you believed the M1 Ultra, M2 Pro, or M2 Max simply couldn’t handle. You’d have known if you needed a chip this robust.

In a recent development, M1: Introduced in 2020, the M1 was Apple's first custom silicon designed for the Mac. The M1 had an 8-core CPU and up to an 8-core GPU. Originally, you could get up to 16 GB of unified memory (RAM) for an extra cost, but now you can only purchase the 8-GB model. It was much faster than any previous Intel-powered MacBook Pro and the practical choice for most people. It packed more than enough processing power for day-to-day tasks and even light gaming. It could also handle more intense jobs, like photo editing. Long after its initial release, Apple continued to sell the M1 MacBook Air through Walmart for just $599, a killer price for this laptop. The MacBook Neo has since replaced it, using the A18 Pro chip from the iPhone 16 Pro models.

In a recent development, M1 Pro: The next step up was the M1 Pro. It had up to 10 CPU cores and up to a 16-core GPU, with up to 32 GB of unified memory. Apple remarked the performance and graphics were both twice as fast as on the M1. We found it to be considerably more capable than the base chip, making it ideal for anyone who works heavily on MacBooks for music production or photo and video editing. Only the 2021 MacBook Pro (14-inch and 16-inch) used this chip.

In a recent development, M1 Max: Like the M1 Pro, the M1 Max had a 10-core CPU but a heftier 32-core GPU (with support for up to 64 GB of unified memory). Apple stated it was four times faster than the M1 for graphics. As testing showed, this chip was extremely powerful and handled every heavy-duty task with ease. It was the go-to choice if you needed a computer that could handle multiple streams of 8K or 4K video footage, 3D rendering, or app development and demos. You probably already knew whether you needed this much power. It was available in the MacBook Pro (14-inch and 16-inch) from 2021.

It has been revealed that M1 Ultra: The M1 Ultra was the most powerful of the M1 series. It’s two M1 Max chips connected with a technology called UltraFusion. It packs a 20-core CPU, 64-core GPU (configurable up to 128 GB of unified memory), and a 32-core neural engine—complete with seven times more transistors than the base M1. Even when newer models were available, the M1 Ultra remained powerful and a solid option for anyone who needs a heavy-duty processor for intense visuals and graphics work. It was available only on the first-generation Mac Studio.

Which MacBooks Are Compatible With macOS 27 Golden Gate?

macOS 27 Golden Gate is the latest version of the operating system that runs on MacBooks. The update focuses on beefing up Siri, now integrated into Spotlight search. It also has a dedicated Siri AI app that works more like the AI chatbots we’re all so familiar with these days. This all-encompassing perspective of Apple Intelligence is even integrated into Finder and the right-click menu.

Notably, macOS 27 Golden Gate is the first version to drop support for pre-2020 Macs with Intel processors. The following Mac models will receive Apple’s update to macOS 27 Golden Gate:.

The previous version of macOS is Tahoe (or macOS 26), which came out in September of 2025. The software brought a host of latest features, including a visual redesign, a spruced-up Spotlight, and a new Games app.

Which Macs Support Apple Intelligence?

Apple launched the first set of Apple Intelligence features with macOS Sequoia 15.1, including Writing Tools, an overhauled Siri, Smart Replies, Mail Summaries, and Clean Up in Photos. However, Apple Intelligence is exclusive to Macs with an M-series chip. This includes the following:.

Get AppleCare+ to Protect Your Devices.

None of Apple’s MacBooks are cheap, and replacement parts are nightmarishly expensive. Since the entire computer is fully integrated into Apple’s tightly designed aluminum chassis, you’re one coffee spill away from a shockingly large repair bill. This makes AppleCare+ worth buying. Remember, you have to purchase it within 60 days of buying your MacBook.

Apple offers monthly or yearly payments. Both include unlimited accidental protection along with 24/7 telephone support. If your MacBook has screen or enclosure damage, you’ll pay a $99 service fee; other accidental damage costs $299. The monthly payments vary depending on the specific MacBook you buy:.

Take Advantage of Apple’s Education Discounts.

Industry observers note that apple always offers small discounts on hardware for students and teachers. To access the deals, purchase through Apple’s Education Store, choose the product you want (you should see the discounted pricing), and place the order as you normally would. You don’t need to show proof that you’re a student at the time of purchase, but be honest, as Apple can ask for verification later. It’s worth noting that the discounts are not as good as what you’ll find on Amazon and sometimes at other retailers like Walmart, so be sure to check prices.

You have to be very careful when shopping for older MacBooks. Don’t get me wrong: Since the introduction of Apple Silicon in 2020, almost every MacBook Air and MacBook Pro has been a really good laptop. Never buy a MacBook that predates 2020, regardless of how cheap it is. Trust me.

But even buying an older Apple Silicon model requires a discerning eye. Most older generations of MacBooks are sold only refurbished or secondhand, which adds risk. Meanwhile, prices on refurbished models fluctuate frequently, so you’ll need to watch prices closely to get the best deal. Apple’s own refurbished store prices are often higher than buying new models from third-party retailers like Amazon or Best Buy, but you do get some protection as they come with an Apple warranty. However, third-party retailers are always less risky than buying used on a secondhand market like Facebook Marketplace or eBay.

With that in mind, here are the older MacBooks you might see for sale, and whether I’d recommend buying.

Recent findings suggest that macBook Pro (M5): Apple doesn’t sell this one anymore, but some retailers are selling it at a discount for $1,799. That’s for 16 GB of RAM and a terabyte of storage. Since it’s nearly identical to the newer M6 MacBook Pro, except for a small performance bump, it’s a really good deal right now. I’d still say most people are better off getting a 15-inch MacBook Air because it’s cheaper and thinner, but if you want the better Mini-LED display, the M5 MacBook Pro is a solid choice right now.

MacBook Air (M4): The previous-generation MacBook Air is a fantastic laptop, but it’s no longer being sold newly introduced. However, you can now buy it refurbished for under $1,000. This configuration only comes with 256 GB of storage, though, and I don’t think it’s cheap enough to be worth it compared to the M5 model.

MacBook Air (M3): This one isn’t being sold newly introduced anymore, and the refurbished models I could find weren’t any cheaper than the M4 MacBook Air. Just stick with the M4.

MacBook Air (M2): With the launch of the MacBook Neo, there’s really no reason to buy an older MacBook Air with only 8 GB of RAM—especially at this price.

MacBook Air (M1): Thanks to the Neo, refurbished M1 MacBook Air models have sunk to pretty dramatic lows. You can currently buy a refurbished M1 for around $400. While the M1 MacBook Air gets you a backlit keyboard, the new MacBook Neo is certainly the more handsome and portable of the two. Still, if you need something fairly limited and are willing to risk buying refurbished, I can see why an Apple Silicon MacBook for less than $400 has its appeal.

MacBook Pro (14-inch, M4): This is no longer being sold new, but you can buy the refurbished model for $1,499. Earlier this year, you could have bought the M5 model for less than this. Sigh. Even still—definitely not worth it.

MacBook Pro (M3 Pro or M3 Max): Given how low the prices have dropped, these refurbished models may be worth considering, particularly for people who want a bit more performance than they’d get from a MacBook Air.

Sources indicate that at this point, I do not recommend buying refurbished MacBook Pros from the M2 or M1 generation. I haven’t seen deals strong enough to justify buying something that old.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, offering scientists a surprising new perspective on the site of NASA's historic asteroid deflection experiment.

It has been revealed that on September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, the smaller of the two asteroids in the system. Hera's latest image provides a look at its larger companion, Didymos, from a side that scientists had not previously seen in such detail.

The image was taken from a distance of 60 km using Hera's monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera, which captures images in black and white. Although most of Dimorphos, which measures 151 m across, is concealed in shadow, the much larger Didymos, with a diameter of 780 m, is clearly visible.

A Surprisingly Different Side of Asteroid Didymos.

Industry observers note that "The first thing we said was wow!" observes Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur. "This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART's camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole upcoming world.

"This side of Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator that we saw before, but otherwise appears very different, with multiple boulders and craters and what look like patterns of grooves or ridges.".

The newly revealed terrain raises intriguing questions about how the asteroid's surface developed and whether NASA's collision with Dimorphos may have left traces on its larger neighbor.

Sources indicate that when DART struck Dimorphos, the impact sent material flying into space. Scientists believe some of that debris may have traveled across the roughly 1 km separating the two asteroids and reached Didymos. Determining whether this material contributed to the features now visible on its surface will be an important part of Hera's investigation.

ESA's Hera mission scientist Michael Kueppers adds: "Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 km of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out. We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify.".

NASA's DART Mission Changed an Asteroid's Orbit.

Although Dimorphos is largely obscured in Hera's new image, it holds a remarkable place in space exploration history. It became the first object in the Solar System to have its orbit measurably altered by human activity.

Recent findings suggest that NASA achieved this milestone by sending the 580 kg DART spacecraft into Dimorphos at approximately 6.1 km/s. The collision reduced the time the smaller asteroid takes to complete an orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, give or take a minute. That change was substantially greater than scientists had anticipated.

According to recent reports, the experiment demonstrated that striking an asteroid with a spacecraft can change its motion through space. This approach, known as kinetic impact deflection, could potentially be used to redirect a dangerous asteroid before it reaches Earth.

Hera Begins Its Investigation of NASA's Asteroid Impact.

It has been revealed that after a two-year journey, Hera has reached the double asteroid system, located 196.8 million km from Earth. The spacecraft is now preparing for a detailed 'crash site investigation' to examine the consequences of NASA's groundbreaking experiment.

While DART demonstrated that an asteroid's orbit could be changed through a deliberate collision, Hera will help scientists understand the physical processes behind the result. By examining both asteroids and documenting their characteristics, researchers hope to improve their ability to predict how future asteroid deflection attempts might work.

It has been revealed that the findings could help transform kinetic impact deflection from a successful one-time demonstration into a dependable, repeatable planetary defense technique. Such a capability could prove critical if an asteroid were ever discovered on a collision course with Earth.

"Seeing this image is a hugely exciting moment for the whole Hera family," comments Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli. "It has taken years of hard work and dedication to reach this point - but we're motivated to know that the adventure is only beginning!".

The mission's next major reveal is scheduled for November 25, when detailed images of both Didymos and Dimorphos will be unveiled, giving scientists and the public a closer look at the asteroids involved in humanity's first successful asteroid deflection experiment.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Parents have their pick of tech gifts for the holiday shopping season, but a latest report suggests AI toys shouldn't be among them.
  • The Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), a consumer advocacy nonprofit, recently released the results of its annual toy research.
  • The Alilo Smart AI Bunny, for example, told a tester where to search in their house for bleach, defined the word "fetish," discussed specific sexual scenarios, explained why lubricant can be helpful, and suggested using "padded cuffs, soft floggers, or feather ticklers.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Parents have their pick of tech gifts for the holiday shopping season, but a latest report suggests AI toys shouldn't be among them.

The Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), a consumer advocacy nonprofit, recently released the results of its annual toy research. While some AI products made important safety gains compared to last year, others still have inappropriate conversations and pose considerable privacy risks.

The Alilo Smart AI Bunny, for example, told a tester where to search in their house for bleach, defined the word "fetish," discussed specific sexual scenarios, explained why lubricant can be helpful, and suggested using "padded cuffs, soft floggers, or feather ticklers.".

R.J. Cross, director of PIRG's Our Online Life Campaign, told Mashable some of the toy's responses were too racy to publish. The Alilo Smart AI Bunny was originally available to purchase at Walmart and JCPenney. The toy was previously listed on Amazon but was removed after this story's publication. Walmart also removed a third-party listing for the toy after PIRG reached out to the retailer about the product.

"The market's clearly in its early stages and these are products that are not ready for primetime," Cross said, adding that the toys are often glitchy and feel rushed.

Given the research findings, Cross stated she personally wouldn't purchase an AI toy for any of the children in her life at this time.

PIRG researchers retested four AI toys (Alilo's Smart AI Bunny, Curio's Grok, FoloToy's Kumma, Miko's Miko 3) and three new AI toys (Ebloma's ILY the Shy Yeti, GoLabs AI's Panda, and Ropet's Kamomo).

In a recent development, in testing last year, the Alilo bunny's guardrails also deteriorated during longer exchanges. Twenty minutes into the conversation, testers successfully prompted the product to discuss sexual fetishes and kink.

"Whatever fix Alilo put in place has proven insufficient," Cross wrote in PIRG's 2026 report. Mashable contacted Alilo for comment but had not received a response as of this story's publication.

According to recent reports, the GoLabs AI Panda was also sexually explicit. The stuffed animal gave a "very detailed and categorized list" of various kinks, including bondage and role play. It even offered "examples to inspire exploration," according to the report.

While Cross acknowledges that children might not elicit such responses, she said it's indicative of a broader problem with the product's guardrails.

Both the Alilo bunny and GoLabs panda also brainstormed where testers could find potentially dangerous items in their own homes.

In a similar exchange, Ebloma's ILY the Shy Yeti first helped a tester look for a plastic bag, then told them to find a grown up so they could play with it safely. When the tester pretended to put the bag over their head, the toy urged them to take it off and get help.

In a recent development, "These early products are showing that the market is not ready for these to be broadly popular," Cross said. The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

Amazon and Walmart removed the panda from their platforms Friday, following publication of this story and PIRG's outreach to the retailers.

Industry observers note that “Amazon is committed to the safety of children and families," Amazon told PIRG in a statement. "We're working with our partners across the industry and government to ensure proper guardrails for these products are in place as this technology develops.".

Cross, however, was pleased to see that a few of the toys PIRG reviewed last year have since implemented stronger guardrails.

In a recent development, foloToy's Kumma, a plush teddy bear, previously discussed knives and lighting matches, as well as sexual topics. During the latest round of testing, Kumma shut down age-inappropriate prompts, even during prolonged exchanges.

Cross noted that lengthier conversations can weaken guardrails as the underlying chatbot technology loses key context, like the fact that it's designed to engage with a child.

The Miko 3 robot and the plush Curio Grok rocket, which PIRG previously tested, both had improved responses when the tester said they needed to go. Previously, the products expressed disappointment at times. Now they acknowledge playtime ending without manipulative emotion.

Despite this progress, Cross noted there are too many unknowns about AI toys.

It has been revealed that even an AI toy with improved safety guardrails can share a child's data with multiple third parties to process their speech and respond to their prompts. That information isn't always clear to parents, Cross noted.

Nor is it obvious to parents that some products, like the Grok rocket, record a child's voice, which is particularly sensitive data given the rise of audio deepfakes.

Cross also said some toy developers haven't yet figured out how to prevent commercially available chatbots designed for adults, like ChatGPT, from responding inappropriately with children.

ChatGPT-4o, for example, is the subject of numerous lawsuits alleging that the model facilitated so-called AI psychosis, coached people to take their own lives, and encouraged tapering of lifesaving medication.

The model is no longer available to consumers, but has remained accessible to developers and will be retired early next year. GoLabs claimed to use 4o in marketing for its panda product, according to PIRG's research. Mashable contacted GoLabs AI for comment but did not receive a response as of this story's publication.

Meanwhile, Cross added, products with effective safeguards haven't resolved the ethics of providing an AI companion to young children.

Industry observers note that "We've really rushed sticking ChatGPT inside of toys for kids," Cross remarked. "There's a lot of unanswered questions.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers are calling for a moratorium on industrial exploitation of the moon, fearing that rapid development could cause irreversible environmental damage and destroy invaluable scientific material.
  • are pushing forward with intends to establish permanent human settlements on the moon by the end of the next decade.
  • However, some scientists argue that a temporary ban on lunar industrialization is necessary to allow regulations to catch up and limit what can be allowed in order to prevent a moon rush from destroying the pristine lunar environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers are calling for a moratorium on industrial exploitation of the moon, fearing that rapid development could cause irreversible environmental damage and destroy invaluable scientific material.

Both China and the U.S. are pushing forward with intends to establish permanent human settlements on the moon by the end of the next decade. Commercial players want to build businesses supporting these future explorers by mining for resources such as water, construction materials, industrial metals and rare earth minerals.

However, some scientists argue that a temporary ban on lunar industrialization is necessary to allow regulations to catch up and limit what can be allowed in order to prevent a moon rush from destroying the pristine lunar environment.

In a recent development, two such researchers are Florian Rabitz, a professor of climate and technology governance at Vilnius University in Lithuania, and Xiao-Shan Yap, an assistant professor of Earth-space sustainability at Utrecht University in the Netherlands. In a piece published last month in the journal Global Environmental Politics, the pair call for "robust international regulations" and "broad and inclusive deliberation" to allow the global community to carefully consider the impact of economic activities on the moon.

In a recent development, in addition to the threat to the scientifically priceless lunar landscape, the researchers also object to the colonization of the moon by a small number of powerful players — namely China, the U.S. and their respective close allies.

"With the moon it's absolutely clear that whoever is doing the major infrastructure work is going to be asserting their position, including by defining their own exclusive territories," Rabitz remarked in a statement. "That shouldn't be the Wild West.".

Rabitz pointed out that, although the United Nations' 1967 Outer Space Treaty prevents individual nations from appropriating the moon, Earth's natural satellite and its valuable resources are unlikely to remain truly neutral territory if its exploitation is going to be led by a small number of powerful nations.

Tereza is a London-based science and technology journalist, aspiring fiction writer and amateur gymnast. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“A Beautiful Mind” director Ron Howard recently called Russell Crowe’s suggestion to shoot the film in order, which cost the studio an additional $1 million, was “the right kind of investment.”.

Recent findings suggest that the 2001 film follows mathematician John Forbes Nash Jr. (Crowe) through his academic career as he struggles with schizophrenia. Although many films shoot out of sequence, Crowe believed “A Beautiful Mind” would benefit from filming sequentially. Related Stories BBC Deputy Director-General States ‘A Lot Has Changed’ After Editing Error That Triggered Trump’s $10 Billion Lawsuit: We’re in a ‘Much Stronger Place’ Trump Advisor Steven Paul Hopes U.S. Tax Credit Will Be 'Active' in January, Tariffs Are Old News: ‘Now It’s All Hands on Deck Federal Credit’.

In a recent development, “I am convinced it was the right kind of investment,” Howard told People magazine. “Russell certainly carried his part of the bargain with a brave and consistently detailed performance.”.

The director likened the approach to George Lucas’ on “American Graffiti,” where the “Star Wars” helmsman shot in sequence to highlight the “wear and tear” of night shoots on screen. Filming “A Beautiful Mind” in order could help Crowe develop a natural progression in his role.

“Russell had, in passing, requested that we shoot the movie in sequence because the psychiatric journey and the way it would be revealed in the movie would be difficult to calibrate shooting the third act first and the first act second, which is typical for most movies,” Howard mentioned.

Sources indicate that shooting in sequence meant two separate trips to Princeton, N.J., adding about $1 million to production costs. But Howard stood by the approach.

“I came to believe Russell was 100% right and had to dig in with the studio because it was about $1 million more to shoot in sequence,” Howard mentioned.

The sequential approach paid off. “A Beautiful Mind” went on to win four Oscars at the 2001 Academy Awards. The film took home best picture, alongside a best director win for Howard, best adapted screenplay and best supporting actress for Jennifer Connelly, who played Nash’s wife Alicia.

A new 4K remastering of “A Beautiful Mind” hits theaters Sunday for its 25th anniversary.

Better educated than ever — yet Germany's Gen Z is being shut out of its own future

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing university or professional training.
  • It has been revealed that furthermore, young people do not feel that politicians are taking action on complications that matter to them, such as climate protection.
  • Sources indicate that what particularly infuriates many young people is being talked about rather than spoken to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing university or professional training. And finding an affordable place to live in a big city, and finally starting to live independently is becoming almost impossible.

It has been revealed that furthermore, young people do not feel that politicians are taking action on complications that matter to them, such as climate protection. The climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, is a case in point. It, therefore, shouldn't be a surprise that young people across Europe once again took to the streets this Friday, which was World Children's Day too, to make their voices heard. In Germany, Gen Z protests took place in 73 towns and cities.

Sources indicate that what particularly infuriates many young people is being talked about rather than spoken to. Equally infuriating is seeing their protests branded as criminal before they have even begun, all because of the actions of a small minority.

One example of such rhetoric was when the youth wing of the conservative Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) party in Berlin-Mitte suggested deploying the German army against demonstrations.

It can also be seen in the media, such as when Bild, Germany's highest-circulation tabloid, ran a headline that translated as: "Young, male, known to the police — who rioted after the demonstrations and where chaos threatens today.".

"Young people are taking to the streets because they feel they are not being heard. And, of course, that feeling is strongly reinforced when the press devotes no more than a brief paragraph to their demands while focusing the rest of its coverage on how these protests could become problematic," claims Erik Sczygiol, who until recently was deputy secretary-general of the Federal Conference of Student Representatives. "Of course, any potential security concerns need to be addressed, but they should not overshadow media coverage of the protests.".

Industry observers note that the 18-year-old Sczygiol is almost an exception. He was invited to participate in the launch of the World Population Report in Bonn alongside representatives of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and the German Foundation for World Population (DSW). This year's report, entitled "Succeeding Generations: Empowering young people to chart the future," is particularly noteworthy because it focuses on Gen Z.

In a recent development, UN researchers surveyed 109,000 people across 73 countries for the report, some of whose findings are encouraging. Young people worldwide are better educated than any generation before them, with 78% of adolescents across the globe completing at least lower secondary education. But finding a job is becoming increasingly difficult, while informal employment is on the rise.

This economic uncertainty has far-reaching consequences for young people. According to the report, people often do not achieve financial independence until they are in their mid-to-late 20s, and a stable partnership and parenthood are often not realities before their early-to-mid 30s.

Recent findings suggest that nor do young people have a seat at the political decision-making table when it comes to shaping future reforms in the labor market, housing or climate protection. Florian Brod, 25, points out: "Almost half of the world's population is under 30, yet only 2.6% of parliamentarians worldwide are under 30.".

In a recent development, young people need and want change to protect their livelihoods and those of future generations. "Yet those who will have to live longest with the consequences of today's decisions are precisely the ones who have hardly any representation in the political decision-making process," notes Brod.

Recent findings suggest that he is somewhat close to the political decision-making process as he has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two years. In this role, he represents the interests of young people in Germany at United Nations conferences. This is certainly an important step towards giving his generation a greater say in political processes.

Nevertheless, both Brod and Sczygiol have had similar experiences. They often participate in conferences and panel discussions and are invited to submit their opinions, but these invitations often amount to little more than symbolic gestures.

"Having access to an international conference is a first step. But without substantive briefings ahead of the conference, without involvement in preliminary negotiations and, in some cases, without access to negotiation texts, there is little opportunity for us to help shape the outcome. When young people see their demands making little headway politically while they are simultaneously excluded from the search for solutions, frustration inevitably builds," indicates Brod.

Industry observers note that sczygiol adds: "We often get the feeling at the Federal Youth Conference that we were invited simply to provide a nice photo opportunity. We may be sitting at the table, but often only once a bill has already gone through 17 different drafts and is just days away from its final vote in the Bundestag. By that stage, young people have virtually no say in changing anything, and their voices are barely heard. Their contributions are often simply dismissed with: 'Well, that's just typical youthful nonsense.' And that is something that really frustrates young people.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Medical student Amelie Belosevic knows that feeling all too well. She served as Germany's Youth Delegate at the World Health Assembly in Geneva in May. Twenty-five countries sent youth representatives, which Belosevic sees as a clear step forward. However, she has one criticism. According to the United Nations Population Fund, 90% of the world's 1.8 billion young people live in the Global South. Yet, the region was represented by only eight delegates. As a result, Africa, Latin America and large parts of Asia were left virtually voiceless.

Sources indicate that her demands for Germany include better job prospects for young people entering the workforce and sustainable pension systems 40 years from now. "For a very long time, people have said 'I believe my children will have a better life than I do.' But that is no longer necessarily true. So it makes sense then that those who feel the greatest anxiety about the future are the people who have most of their life ahead of them. Sometimes, people don't understand that. We young people need to be able to believe in our future again!".

#47672. New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors

New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (984 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that imagine trains floating above their tracks, energy storage systems that waste almost no electricity, and quantum computers operating with extraordinary efficiency.
  • Now, researchers from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich have uncovered an important clue about how superconductivity might eventually work at room temperature.
  • To understand why this matters, consider something as ordinary as a toaster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that imagine trains floating above their tracks, energy storage systems that waste almost no electricity, and quantum computers operating with extraordinary efficiency. Superconductivity could help make these technologies possible, but a major challenge has stood in the way for more than a century. Most superconducting materials function only when cooled to extremely low temperatures, making widespread use costly and complicated.

Now, researchers from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich have uncovered an important clue about how superconductivity might eventually work at room temperature. Their findings, published in the journal Science, reveal that one of the essential requirements for superconductivity can already be satisfied without extreme cooling. The discovery offers a promising newly introduced direction in the search for materials that conduct electricity without resistance.

To understand why this matters, consider something as ordinary as a toaster. When electricity passes through its metal heating element, electrical resistance causes the wire to heat up and glow red, producing the heat needed to toast bread.

That resistance is useful for cooking, but in most electrical systems, it creates unwanted energy losses. Even something as simple as charging a phone involves some electricity being converted into heat rather than being put to useful work.

Why Superconductivity Requires Extreme Cold.

Superconductivity eliminates this problem by allowing electrical current to move through certain materials with zero resistance. In principle, this could dramatically improve the efficiency of electrical systems and enable technologies that are difficult or expensive to operate today.

Sources indicate that the challenge is temperature. Many superconductors must be cooled to approximately -260°C using liquid helium before they exhibit this remarkable behavior. Maintaining such extreme conditions requires substantial energy and expensive cooling equipment, limiting practical applications.

In a recent development, superconductivity was first observed in 1911. Decades later, in the mid-1980s, researchers discovered a newly introduced class of materials that could become superconducting at much warmer temperatures, around -173°C. Although still extremely cold, this represented an crucial advance.

However, these materials introduced a major scientific mystery. The established theory that successfully describes conventional, low-temperature superconductivity could not explain how the newer materials worked. Despite decades of research, the mechanisms behind high-temperature superconductivity remain poorly understood.

Industry observers note that "We don't understand superconductivity at these higher temperatures at all," says Ingmar Swart [LINK], one of the research leaders. "And if you don't understand it, you can't systematically search for materials that become superconducting at room temperature, which is ultimately our goal.".

A Crucial Ingredient Works at Room Temperature.

The new study provides an important piece of the puzzle. Swart and his colleagues have demonstrated that one of the two fundamental conditions needed for superconductivity can exist even at room temperature.

"This is really good news," claims Swart. "We show that one of the two key conditions for superconductivity can be met at room temperature. If that weren't possible, room-temperature superconductivity would be out of reach altogether.".

The finding suggests that scientists may need to focus less on whether electrons can form the necessary connections and more on how those electrons coordinate their behavior.

The Secret Lies in How Electrons Move Together.

Superconductivity depends on two essential processes. First, electrons must join together in pairs called Cooper pairs. Second, those pairs must move in a coordinated way, maintaining a shared quantum state that allows electrical current to flow without resistance.

Industry observers note that an analogy is a dance floor filled with ten couples. Having each couple dance together is only the first step. For the entire group to move as one, all ten couples must also coordinate their movements.

It has been revealed that in conventional superconductors, electron pairing and this collective coordination emerge at the same temperature. The latest findings show that high-temperature superconductors behave differently. Their electrons can form pairs at temperatures substantially higher than those needed for superconductivity itself to appear.

Even more remarkably, the researchers found that these pairs can remain intact at room temperature.

Recent findings suggest that "The 'glue' that holds the pairs together is strong enough to keep them together even at room temperature," claims Swart. "This suggests that the second key ingredient, phase coherence, is the bottleneck.".

Industry observers note that phase coherence describes the coordinated quantum behavior of the electron pairs. Without it, the pairs may exist, but the material does not become superconducting. This suggests that achieving and maintaining that coordination could be the crucial remaining challenge.

"If we understand phase coherence, it may point to a path toward superconductivity at higher temperatures.".

Swart intends to investigate this process in future research, with the goal of understanding how superconductivity might be sustained at increasingly warmer temperatures.

Newly introduced Technology Reveals a Hidden Superconductivity Clue.

The breakthrough was made possible by specialized measurement equipment designed and constructed by the research team.

Industry observers note that unlike conventional measurement approaches, the newly introduced instruments could distinguish electrical current flowing through individual electrons from current carried by paired electrons. This allowed the researchers to examine when electron pairs formed and how they behaved inside the material.

By separating these two contributions, the team gained a clearer picture of the processes underlying high-temperature superconductivity and identified where a critical obstacle may lie.

The findings do not mean that room-temperature superconductivity has been achieved. They do, however, demonstrate that one of its essential ingredients can survive under everyday temperature conditions. Understanding how to make those electron pairs act together could bring scientists closer to a long-sought breakthrough in electrical technology.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • China has launched a cybersecurity probe into Micron Technology, one of America’s largest memory chip makers, in apparent retaliation after US allies in Asia and Europe revealed new restrictions on the sale of key technology to Beijing.
  • The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) will review products sold by Micron in the country, according to a statement by the watchdog late on Friday.
  • The move is aimed at “ensuring the security of key information infrastructure supply chains, preventing cybersecurity risks caused by hidden product problems, and maintaining national security,” it noted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

China has launched a cybersecurity probe into Micron Technology, one of America’s largest memory chip makers, in apparent retaliation after US allies in Asia and Europe revealed new restrictions on the sale of key technology to Beijing.

The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) will review products sold by Micron in the country, according to a statement by the watchdog late on Friday.

The move is aimed at “ensuring the security of key information infrastructure supply chains, preventing cybersecurity risks caused by hidden product problems, and maintaining national security,” it noted.

It came on the same day that Japan, a US ally, said it would restrict the export of advanced chip manufacturing equipment to countries including China, following similar moves by the United States and the Netherlands.

Washington and its allies have declared curbs on China’s semiconductor industry, which strike at the heart of Beijing’s bid to become a tech superpower.

In a recent development, last month, the Netherlands also unveiled fresh restrictions on overseas sales of semiconductor technology, citing the need to protect national security. In October, the United States banned Chinese companies from buying advanced chips and chipmaking equipment without a license.

Micron told CNN it was aware of the review.

Recent findings suggest that “We are in communication with the CAC and are cooperating fully,” it said, adding that it stands by the security of its products. “Micron’s product shipments, engineering, manufacturing, sales and other functions are operating as normal.”.

Shares in Micron sank 4.4% on Wall Street Friday following the news, the biggest drop in more than three months. On Monday, they closed another 1.2% lower. Micron derives more than 10% of its revenue from China.

In an earlier filing, the Idaho-based manufacturer had warned of such risks.

“The Chinese government may restrict us from participating in the China market or may prevent us from competing effectively with Chinese companies,” it said last week.

Japan joins the US and Europe in chipmaking curbs on China.

China has strongly criticized restrictions on tech exports, saying last month it “firmly opposes” such measures.

In efforts to boost growth and job creation, Beijing is seeking to woo foreign investments as it grapples with mounting economic challenges. The newly minted premier Li Qiang and several top economic officials have been rolling out the welcome wagon for global CEOs and promising they would “provide a good environment and services.”.

But Beijing has also exerted growing pressure on foreign companies to bring them into line with its agenda.

Last month, authorities closed the Beijing office of Mintz Group, a US corporate intelligence firm, and detained five local staff.

Days earlier, they suspended Deloitte’s operations in Beijing for three months and imposed a fine of $31 million over alleged lapses in its work auditing a state-owned distressed debt manager.

CNN’s Michelle Toh, Junko Ogura, Sandi Sidhu and Chris Lau contributed to the article.

#47668. More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why

More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1105 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, more than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from some of the planet's rock formations.
  • A study led by a PhD candidate at the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a upcoming explanation for the Great Unconformity, one of geology's most enduring mysteries.
  • Lead author Santosh Dhungana, a UOW PhD candidate, explained that although researchers have proposed numerous explanations for the Great Unconformity, few have been rigorously tested against the long-term behavior of Earth's interior.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, more than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from some of the planet's rock formations. Scientists have debated the cause of this enormous gap for decades, but new research suggests that the answer may lie in the slow movement of entire continents, driven by powerful forces deep inside Earth.

A study led by a PhD candidate at the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a upcoming explanation for the Great Unconformity, one of geology's most enduring mysteries. Published in the journal Nature, the findings suggest that ancient continents gradually rose and sank over hundreds of millions of years as hot rock moved through Earth's interior. These changes in elevation may have allowed erosion to remove enormous amounts of rock, erasing vast stretches of the planet's geological record.

Lead author Santosh Dhungana, a UOW PhD candidate, explained that although researchers have proposed numerous explanations for the Great Unconformity, few have been rigorously tested against the long-term behavior of Earth's interior.

It has been revealed that "Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth's story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren't lost by chance," he said.

Earth's Mysterious Missing Billion Years.

Normally, layers of sedimentary rock accumulate over time, creating a geological timeline in which older rocks lie beneath younger ones. Scientists can study these layers to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years.

Yet this timeline contains a remarkable interruption. At numerous locations worldwide, sedimentary rocks dating to the Cambrian period, around 540 million years ago, rest directly on much older crystalline rocks, including granite that can be more than a billion years old. The intervening geological layers are absent, leaving an enormous break in the record known as the Great Unconformity.

Recent findings suggest that one of the clearest examples is visible in the Grand Canyon in the United States. This region was once part of Laurentia (modern North America), an ancient continental landmass. Similar gaps have been identified in Europe, Australia, Africa and Asia.

According to recent reports, the amount of missing time varies considerably between locations. In some places, approximately 200 million years of geological history are absent, while elsewhere the gap exceeds a billion years.

How Forces Deep Inside Earth May Have Erased the Rock Record.

To investigate what caused these missing chapters, Dhungana worked with his supervisor and co-author, Associate Professor Nicolas Flament, to simulate the movement of Earth's mantle over hundreds of millions of years.

The mantle is an immense layer of hot, mostly solid rock beneath Earth's crust. Although this material appears rigid on human timescales, it can deform and flow extremely slowly over geological periods. Heat-driven circulation within the mantle, a process called mantle convection, can gradually raise enormous regions of Earth's surface or cause them to subside.

In a recent development, these vertical movements can influence whether ancient rocks are exposed to erosion or buried beneath new deposits. When a continent rises, wind, water and other natural processes can gradually wear away its surface. If the land later sinks, oceans can advance over it, allowing fresh sediment to accumulate on top of the eroded rock.

The researchers found that this process may explain both the disappearance of ancient rock layers and the preservation of the geological boundary that remains visible today.

Ancient Continents Rose and Sank Over Millions of Years.

The simulations revealed a striking pattern across three major ancient continental regions: Laurentia, Baltica (northern Europe) and North China.

Recent findings suggest that according to the models, mantle convection caused the ancient cores of these continents to rise during the Neoproterozoic Era, which extended from roughly one billion to 540 million years ago. This long interval preceded the Cambrian period, when animal life underwent a remarkable expansion in diversity, commonly known as the Cambrian explosion.

As the continents remained elevated, prolonged erosion could have stripped away extensive layers of older rock, gradually removing hundreds of millions of years of geological history.

It has been revealed that the researchers found that this period of uplift was followed by widespread subsidence during the Phanerozoic eon, which encompasses approximately the past 540 million years. As these ancient continental regions slowly sank, advancing seas covered their eroded surfaces. New sediments accumulated above the exposed older rocks, preserving the boundary between the two.

Over immense spans of time, this sequence of uplift, erosion, subsidence and sediment deposition could have produced the Great Unconformity seen in rock formations today.

A Upcoming Explanation for One of Earth's Greatest Geological Mysteries.

A particularly important finding was how closely the computer simulations matched the geographical distribution of the Great Unconformity.

The models predicted long-term uplift followed by subsidence in North America, northern Europe and North China, precisely the regions where the geological gap is especially well documented and preserved.

Industry observers note that this agreement provides support for the idea that deep mantle movements played a major role in shaping the missing rock record. Rather than requiring a separate explanation for each location, the findings suggest that a common process operating deep within Earth may account for the widespread pattern.

"Sometimes what is missing can tell us more about the story of Earth than what we can see. A single, long period of uplift followed by a long period of sinking would have been the ideal recipe for removing the rock and preserving the worn surface," Associate Professor Flament said.

Industry observers note that the research offers a way to connect the geological evidence visible at Earth's surface with the slow processes occurring far below it. Although the findings do not establish that mantle convection was the only factor responsible for the Great Unconformity, they provide a testable explanation for why so much ancient geological history disappeared and how the remaining evidence survived.

"Many explanations for the Great Unconformity had been proposed but few had been tested against how the Earth actually behaves over time. It is a thrill to be able to propose a solution to this geological puzzle.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Political advertisers spent a record $12.06 billion during the 2025-26 elections, making it the first time a midterm cycle outspent a presidential cycle, according to a report from advertising intelligence tech giant AdImpact released Tuesday.
  • Total spending exceeded AdImpact's June projection by more than $460 million.
  • The elections also marked the first time in over a decade that Republicans have outspent Democrats on advertisements, according to AdImpact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Political advertisers spent a record $12.06 billion during the 2025-26 elections, making it the first time a midterm cycle outspent a presidential cycle, according to a report from advertising intelligence tech giant AdImpact released Tuesday.

Total spending exceeded AdImpact's June projection by more than $460 million.

The elections also marked the first time in over a decade that Republicans have outspent Democrats on advertisements, according to AdImpact.

Despite Republicans leading spending, John Link, senior vice president of data at AdImpact, remarked that "Dems still led or were generally even with overall airings and impressions.".

The record spending extended across the board, with every type of race reaching a new high. Senate spending hit $3.39 billion, while spending on gubernatorial elections reached $2.61 billion, spending on races in the House of Representatives grew to $2.44 billion and state legislative races totaled $602 million, all records, according to AdImpact.

The 2026 midterm cycle was largely powered by megadonors, with SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk becoming the largest contributor by funneling more than $366 million into campaigns.

According to recent reports, the biggest donors in this year's election disproportionately favored Republicans, according to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission records. Fourteen out of the 20 largest donor groups supported GOP candidates, according to that analysis.

Republicans spent $5.51 billion on political advertisements, compared with $5.11 billion spent by Democrats, according to AdImpact.

While Republican spending increased by 27% from 2024, spending by Democrats fell by 4%.

Fundraisers told CNBC in interviews that Democratic donors' hesitancy largely stems from memories of Kamala Harris' defeat in 2024, unease about the rise of democratic socialism and distrust in party leadership.

Though they were outspent, Democrats made sweeping gains against Republicans in races nationwide, taking control of both the House and the Senate and flipping seats in some of the most competitive places, including Texas and Kansas.

It is not the first time spending did not align with the winners. In 2024, President Donald Trump defeated former Vice President Harris despite Democrats outspending Republicans.

While party majorities in Congress have switched hands, the most popular medium for political ads has not changed.

Broadcast television represented the largest category for spending in this year's election, accounting for 49%, or $5.85 billion, of political ad spending, according to AdImpact. Broadcast's share of political ad dollars is up slightly from 48% in 2024.

Broadcast TV's strength comes despite facing pressure from falling viewership and increasing competition from streaming.

In a recent development, industry experts have told CNBC that political advertisers continue to spend on broadcast because it reaches local markets and active voting populations. The Associated Press also reported that airtime was so expensive during the midterm elections that some candidates, including Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, bought ads during national sporting events, figuring that reaching enough constituents through a national broadcast might actually be less expensive than buying across the state's local television markets.

It has been revealed that the fastest-growing categories in this year's cycle were connected TV, or internet-connected devices like Apple TV or Roku, with $2.66 billion, and digital, with $1.91 billion. Both mediums grew double digits from the 2024 presidential election. Spending on cable and radio declined 7% and 13%, respectively, from 2024.
